commits.message:
fix(ai): persist post-resume text, stop attach self-duplication in chat sync

Two defects found live-testing multi-window chat sync:

1. Reload lost the final answer of any HITL turn. A turn that suspends
   mid-message (frontend tool / artifact show) flushes the PARTIAL assistant
   row at suspend time; at resume-finish Mastra re-saves the same message id
   with the full part list — and appendMessage's ignoreDuplicates upsert
   silently dropped it. saveMessages now routes re-saves of existing
   assistant/tool messages through updateMessageParts (no-op when parts are
   unchanged); user re-saves stay insert-once so folded attachment parts
   survive.

2. The sending window duplicated its own final message up to 4x. The artifact
   auto-resume dispatch leaves submitInFlight false, so the window's realtime
   'running' signal attached it to the run its own POST was already streaming
   — and at run end, three signals raced through resumeActiveRun before the
   loop's async 'running' flag was set, each replaying the full event log.
   Three guards: skip attaching to the locally-streamed run (client resume
   reuses the client-supplied runId), a synchronous dispatch latch, and the
   replay filter now refuses text for any message id the lane already renders.

Also: recoveryAttemptedRef is set BEFORE launching from the realtime path
(the loop's own submitStatus flip re-ran the mount effect, which aborted the
attach it was reacting to — second window never streamed), the mount effect
no longer aborts a streaming loop on dep changes, and the thread-watch
realtime channel subscribes once per (client, thread) instead of resubscribing
every render — signals landing in the resubscribe gaps were lost.

Verified in-browser: artifact flow renders once in the sending window
(recovery log shows only 'skipped: locally streamed run'), persisted parts
carry the trailing text, second-window live streaming intact. 698 + 774
tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
refactor(ai): user-turn echo as protocol-native role:user text messages

The CUSTOM engenty.user_message event reinvented something AG-UI already
specifies: TEXT_MESSAGE_START carries a role union that includes "user".
The run stream now echoes the user turn as a standard role:"user" text trio,
and the custom event + its client-side synthesis are deleted.

- conversation reducer: upsertStreamedMessage honors the START event's role
  (unknown/missing roles stay assistant; tool-call paths unchanged). User
  messages are write-once in the lane — the SENDING window holds the
  optimistic user message under the same id, and the echo's delta must not
  double its text (the echo also flows through the sender's own POST stream).
- attached-window replay needs no special case anymore: the trio passes the
  same per-message gating as assistant text (admitted when neither snapshot
  nor lane has the id) and the lane renders the user bubble natively.

Verified live: second window renders the user bubble + streamed reply from
the native events, event log seq 1-3 = TEXT_MESSAGE_START(role user)/CONTENT/
END, no duplication in the sending window. 701 + 774 tests green.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(ai): attached windows lose the user turn — close the attach seam, unify user message id

Two stacked defects made a second window consistently render an empty user
bubble (and never heal after the run finished):

1. Attach seam: the run stream routes subscribed to the live bus and then
   replayed persisted rows — an event published before the subscribe but
   committed after the read arrived through neither source. Persistence lags
   publish (unawaited inserts + delta coalescing), and the user-turn trio is
   emitted exactly in that window. run-event-bus now keeps a full in-memory
   event buffer per live run; both attach routes read it in the same tick as
   the subscribe, so live runs are served seamlessly from memory (DB replay
   remains for non-live runs, and for the capped-buffer prefix).

commits.message:
fix(ai-ui): attached windows stop duplicating the current turn; artifact card + pane survive reload/sync

Three live-testing defects from the D7 multi-window work, all client-side:

1) Duplicated streaming in attached windows. Mastra's session stream ids and
   its persisted MessageList ids are independently generated (structural in
   1.55 — createEmptyAssistantMessage rotates a fresh generateId per step, and
   the resume re-save matches rows by the Mastra id, so server-side adoption
   like the user-id fix would break suspend/resume updateMessageParts). Mastra
   also flushes the partial assistant row after EVERY tool call, so a mid-turn
   attach saw the turn twice under two ids that no dedupe could match:
   - partitionSnapshotForRunAttach: rows persisted BY the attached run
     (created_at >= run start) are replay-owned — dropped from the attach
     snapshot and purged from a reload-hydrated lane; the replay re-streams
     them. Rows older than the run (a resume's pre-suspend flush — resume is a
     NEW run, seq restarts at 0, never re-delivers) are kept.
   - shouldApplyTerminalRunMessagesSnapshot: the count-based gate was blind to
     the id split (a lane holding BOTH copies is LONGER than truth, heal
     rejected forever). Text compare on the last assistant instead; used by
     the terminal re-sync and a new post-attach authoritative re-sync so every
     attached run ends on DB identity (and the coalescer's final flush racing
     RUN_FINISHED just defers the heal instead of losing text).

2) Empty artifact pane in the passive window: the active-artifact signal could
   outrun the tenant-wide ai.artifact invalidation, activating a tab the stale
   list didn't carry. The pane handler now invalidates artifactsQueryRoot on
   the same signal.

3) Artifact card folded into "Used N tools" after reload: live streaming
   splits a turn across rotated assistant messages (tools after that
   message's last text -> inline card), but the persisted row coalesces the
   turn into ONE message (tools before the last text -> collapsed timeline).
   New `standalone` flag on ToolCallUiRegistration + hasStandaloneToolCallUi
   in the transcript escape list; set on the artifact and generative-UI cards.

Live-verified by Matthias with two windows (no duplication during/after the
turn, pane syncs with content, card survives reload). 183 copilot + 150
apps-ai/artifacts + 23 gating tests green; recovery-test fixtures moved run
start after the fixture rows to keep exercising the pre-run hydration path,
plus a new purge regression test.

specifies: TEXT_MESSAGE_START carries a role union that includes "user".

  messages are write-once in the lane — the SENDING window holds the
  optimistic user message under the same id, and the echo's delta must not
  double its text (the echo also flows through the sender's own POST stream).

  same per-message gating as assistant text (admitted when neither snapshot
  nor lane has the id) and the lane renders the user bubble natively.

the native events, event log seq 1-3 = TEXT_MESSAGE_START(role user)/CONTENT/
END, no duplication in the sending window. 701 + 774 tests green.

commits.message: persist post-resume text, stop attach self-duplication in chat sync
commits.body:
Two defects found live-testing multi-window chat sync:

1. Reload lost the final answer of any HITL turn. A turn that suspends
   mid-message (frontend tool / artifact show) flushes the PARTIAL assistant
   row at suspend time; at resume-finish Mastra re-saves the same message id
   with the full part list — and appendMessage's ignoreDuplicates upsert
   silently dropped it. saveMessages now routes re-saves of existing
   assistant/tool messages through updateMessageParts (no-op when parts are
   unchanged); user re-saves stay insert-once so folded attachment parts
   survive.

2. The sending window duplicated its own final message up to 4x. The artifact
   auto-resume dispatch leaves submitInFlight false, so the window's realtime
   'running' signal attached it to the run its own POST was already streaming
   — and at run end, three signals raced through resumeActiveRun before the
   loop's async 'running' flag was set, each replaying the full event log.
   Three guards: skip attaching to the locally-streamed run (client resume
   reuses the client-supplied runId), a synchronous dispatch latch, and the
   replay filter now refuses text for any message id the lane already renders.

footers.value:
recoveryAttemptedRef is set BEFORE launching from the realtime path
(the loop's own submitStatus flip re-ran the mount effect, which aborted the
attach it was reacting to — second window never streamed), the mount effect
no longer aborts a streaming loop on dep changes, and the thread-watch
realtime channel subscribes once per (client, thread) instead of resubscribing
every render — signals landing in the resubscribe gaps were lost.

Verified in-browser: artifact flow renders once in the sending window
(recovery log shows only 'skipped: locally streamed run'), persisted parts
carry the trailing text, second-window live streaming intact. 698 + 774
tests green.

commits.message: parallel live streaming into attached chat windows
commits.body:
A second window (or a reloaded one) attaching to an in-flight run previously
showed nothing until the run finished: the attach filter dropped ALL
TEXT_MESSAGE_* events (the "DB snapshot owns text" rule), and the user turn
existed nowhere the attacher could see it before the end-of-turn flush.

- Server: emit a CUSTOM engenty.user_message event (client message id + text)
  right after RUN_STARTED, so attachers can render the user bubble live.
- Client: replace the blanket text drop with a per-message replay filter —
  messages the DB snapshot already carries stay snapshot-owned (no partial-
  flush doubling), messages the snapshot has never seen stream live, which is

  event with id-dedupe against the lane.

at +0.01s and 53 text deltas concurrently with the originating window's
stream; both received RUN_FINISHED in the same instant. 13 route + 697 ai-ui
tests green.

commits.message: durable chat run tracking, fail-loud choice resolution, cross-window sync
commits.body:
Chat runs executed durably but invisibly: the conversation lane never wrote
ai.agent_run / ai.agent_run_event (the session run tracker was wired into the
headless, delegate, and action lanes only). A reloaded client listing session
runs found nothing to reattach to, and a second window on the same thread had
nothing to discover — messages sent before a reload looked lost even though
the run completed and persisted server-side.

- Wire createSessionRunTracker into startConversationRun and
  resumeConversationRun: the tracker publishes to the in-process bus with the
  same seq it persists, so reload/other windows list the run and replay
  ?since=. Run rows are closed in finally (waiting -> requires_action,
  failed -> failed, aborted -> cancelled, else completed) with token usage.
- Client recovery hook: when a realtime signal lands and no run is live, apply
  the persisted transcript whenever it is ahead of the in-memory lane (a
  SUCCEEDED run previously applied nothing — only cancelled/failed unflushed
  text was handled), and sync the open-interrupt chip from thread metadata so
  a decision answered in another window clears everywhere.
- Decision resumes no longer silently deny on an id-only payload:
  resolveDecisionResumeChoice matches choice_id against the interrupt's own
  choices (label recovered when known); an unknown id is rejected with
  400 agent_threads.unresolvedChoice instead of being read as "not approved".

Verified live: kill connection mid-stream -> fresh client finds the running
run and replays RUN_STARTED -> full text -> RUN_FINISHED; decision interrupts
land requires_action; 771 apps/ai + 695 ai-ui tests green.

commits.message: rename thread/session DAL, routes, and service layer

footers.value:
the DB was renamed agent_session -> thread and agent_session_run
-> agent_run, but the TypeScript layer never followed. This lands three
of the sized slices from the infra audit's consolidation path:

- DAL (apps/ai/src/dal/agent-sessions/ -> dal/threads/): ThreadRow,
  ThreadMessageRow, AgentRunRow, ThreadStore, createThreadStore with
  Thread-named methods (getThread, upsertThread, listThreadsForUser,
  etc.) and matching return shapes.
- Routes (agent-sessions-routes.ts / agent-session-runs-routes.ts ->
  thread-routes.ts / thread-run-routes.ts): registerThreadRoutes,
  registerThreadRunRoutes, onThreadPersisted/onThreadDeleted callbacks.
  URL paths already said /threads; only the code names catch up.
- Service (session-service.ts): createThreadService/ThreadService,
  AiService.sessions -> AiService.threads, and the six thread-CRUD
  methods (listThreads, createThread, getThread, updateThread,
  deleteThread(s)).

Deliberately NOT renamed — different concepts, not the Thread entity:
AiSessionScope/AiScopeCredential (the caller's auth scope), the live
in-memory ConversationSession in session-park.ts (still non-durable,
tracked separately), CascadeSessionScope (a voice-call session), and
AiSessionError/AiSessionErrorCode (already emits correct agent_threads.*
codes; renaming the wrapper class is a smaller follow-up).

Wire contracts preserved: JSON response bodies still key off `session`/
`sessions` (packages/ai-ui and modules/engenty-copilot parse these) —
only the internal service-layer variable names changed, remapped at
each response boundary.

Typecheck steady at the pre-existing apps/ai baseline (174 errors, all
predating this change, confirmed via diff). Full suite: 127 files /
741 tests green.

Remaining from the TRK-08 map: modules/engenty-copilot server + UI and
packages/ai-ui's stragglers (frontend side of this same facade).

commits.message:
fix(ci): deploy step reaches its SSH fallback again

v0.1.96 built all five images and then shipped no deploy. The step declares
`set -uo pipefail` and guards every failure explicitly — but Actions runs it
with `bash -e`, which the step inherits. The Coolify API call timed out (the
runner IP is not on the allowlist, so this path is EXPECTED to fail and hand
over to SSH), curl wrote no body, and the unguarded `cat /tmp/deploy.json`
tripped -e — killing the step before the fallback it was falling back to ever
ran. Prod stayed on 0.1.95 until the deploy was triggered by hand.

`set +e` makes the step's explicit-guard style actually hold, and the response
body is printed defensively since a timeout leaves no file. The closing ssh is
still the last command, so a genuinely failed deploy still fails the job.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(security): run the shared policy on the in-process gateway caller

`evaluatePolicy` has been authoritative on all three HTTP transports since
D2, but the two in-process dispatch paths executed module operation handlers
with no policy at all: no capability check, no `requiresApproval`, no profile
policies. A module calling another module was an unguarded lane, and the two
spot fixes on 39576462b were point defenses at two call sites.

`createApi`'s `callGatewayMethod` now runs the same gate before dispatch, on
both the module-operation branch and the core-host-method fallback. Deny
throws a typed `InProcessPolicyError`, which degrades the way an absent module
already does at every existing call site. `require_approval` cannot answer 202
mid-handler, so it resolves as: covering grant (spent by evaluatePolicy, as at
the HTTP edge) -> the outer edge was itself approval-gated and passed -> deny.

Approved-edge state and the caller's real principal travel in a WeakMap keyed
by the auth object core hands the handler, not as a field on
`PluginAuthContext`: a module cannot forge either by writing a property, and
the gate re-evaluates the SAME principal the outer edge did -- moduleIds,
scopes, taskId and sessionId do not survive that projection, so grant lookup
would otherwise silently differ between edges.

Also here, because the gate depends on them:

- plugin-http was dropping `principalType`/`agentId` from the auth it gives
  handlers, so every nested call from an HTTP route would have re-evaluated as
  an ordinary user -- the one principal that never escalates.
- `method-invoker.ts` and the dashboard's `createCallGatewayMethod` had no
  callers at all. Deleted rather than folded, per the no-fallbacks doctrine.
- An `InProcessPolicyError` that escapes a handler answers 403
  `in_process_policy_denied` instead of falling through to a 500.
- The projects portal states its authority for the anonymous visitor
  (service principal, `module.tasks.write`) instead of passing an empty
  context the gate would have to guess about.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message: run the shared policy on the in-process gateway caller
commits.body:
`evaluatePolicy` has been authoritative on all three HTTP transports since
D2, but the two in-process dispatch paths executed module operation handlers
with no policy at all: no capability check, no `requiresApproval`, no profile
policies. A module calling another module was an unguarded lane, and the two
spot fixes on 39576462b were point defenses at two call sites.

`createApi`'s `callGatewayMethod` now runs the same gate before dispatch, on
both the module-operation branch and the core-host-method fallback. Deny
throws a typed `InProcessPolicyError`, which degrades the way an absent module
already does at every existing call site. `require_approval` cannot answer 202
mid-handler, so it resolves as: covering grant (spent by evaluatePolicy, as at
the HTTP edge) -> the outer edge was itself approval-gated and passed -> deny.

Approved-edge state and the caller's real principal travel in a WeakMap keyed
by the auth object core hands the handler, not as a field on
`PluginAuthContext`: a module cannot forge either by writing a property, and
the gate re-evaluates the SAME principal the outer edge did -- moduleIds,
scopes, taskId and sessionId do not survive that projection, so grant lookup
would otherwise silently differ between edges.

Also here, because the gate depends on them:

- plugin-http was dropping `principalType`/`agentId` from the auth it gives
  handlers, so every nested call from an HTTP route would have re-evaluated as
  an ordinary user -- the one principal that never escalates.
- `method-invoker.ts` and the dashboard's `createCallGatewayMethod` had no
  callers at all. Deleted rather than folded, per the no-fallbacks doctrine.
- An `InProcessPolicyError` that escapes a handler answers 403
  `in_process_policy_denied` instead of falling through to a 500.
- The projects portal states its authority for the anonymous visitor
  (service principal, `module.tasks.write`) instead of passing an empty
  context the gate would have to guess about.

commits.message: deploy step reaches its SSH fallback again
commits.body:
v0.1.96 built all five images and then shipped no deploy. The step declares
`set -uo pipefail` and guards every failure explicitly — but Actions runs it
with `bash -e`, which the step inherits. The Coolify API call timed out (the
runner IP is not on the allowlist, so this path is EXPECTED to fail and hand
over to SSH), curl wrote no body, and the unguarded `cat /tmp/deploy.json`
tripped -e — killing the step before the fallback it was falling back to ever
ran. Prod stayed on 0.1.95 until the deploy was triggered by hand.

`set +e` makes the step's explicit-guard style actually hold, and the response
body is printed defensively since a timeout leaves no file. The closing ssh is
still the last command, so a genuinely failed deploy still fails the job.

The plugin runtime callGatewayMethod dispatches module operation handlers
without evaluatePolicy, so gated target ops lose their capability check
and approval requirement on nested cross-module calls.

  gate of its own at all.

  escalation; covered by a new 403 test.

commits.message:
fix(release): module publish survives the GitHub Packages secondary rate limit

v0.1.95 published 25 of 33 modules and then took a 403 "You have exceeded a
secondary rate limit" on @engenty/projects. The run aborted there, and the
registry had no way back to consistent: the script had no retry, and a plain
re-run dies on the first already-published package with EPUBLISHCONFLICT
(workflow_dispatch only ever dry-runs, so there is no manual re-publish path
either).

- a secondary-rate-limit 403 now backs off (30s → 5min, 5 attempts) and retries
- an already-published version is a SKIP, not an error, so re-running the same
  version completes the tail instead of starting over
- everything else still throws — a real publish failure must stay loud
- each module prints its outcome as it goes, so a run that dies partway still
  says what landed (the v0.1.95 log only revealed that by accident)

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
refactor(ai)!: delete the unwired workspace-agent track and tool_profile

`assembleWorkspaceAgent` and `WorkspaceBackedAgentRegistry` were a second agent
assembly stack, built alongside the live one and never wired: zero callers, zero
production references, reachable only through two barrel re-exports. The live
path is `assembleDynamicAgent` over the composite `AiRegistry`. The "Module/core
tools still resolve through the optional legacy AiRegistry seam until W4" comment
lived in the dead copy, and `WorkspaceBackedAgentRegistry.getTool()` returning
undefined was that seam — in a provider no composite stack contains. There is no
W4 to schedule here, only a duplicate to remove.

`tool_profile` went with it. It was designed as a deny-by-default tool ceiling
"regardless of what is stored in the agent's config row", but all three legs are
missing: the only enforcement lived in the dead assembler, `ai.engenty_ai_agents`
has no `tool_profile` column so it cannot round-trip, and the one agent that
declared it (`knowledge-base.answers`) is a module agent served from code through
ModuleProvider and never persisted — so there is no stored row to clamp. Its
declared toolIds already equal the allowlist exactly. Reviving it means building
the column and the enforcement, which is different work from keeping the husk.

`tool-profiles.test.ts` stayed green because it reimplemented the filter in the
test rather than calling shipped code — the reason this went unnoticed. The
registrar test keeps the assertion that actually binds now (the answers agent
declares only the two scoped read tools) and says so.

Deleted: assemble-workspace-agent.ts, workspace-agent-registry.ts,
tool-profiles.ts, tool-profiles.test.ts, agentToolProfileSchema/AgentToolProfile
and the tool_profile field from AgentConfig + the workspace contract.

apps/ai workspace suite 727 green, knowledge-base 273 green, ai-core 243 green;
no new typecheck errors (apps/ai's pre-existing debt unchanged).

commits.message:
refactor(ai)!: one workspace shape — named mounts, no unscoped fallback

`createEngentyAgentWorkspace` built a Workspace two ways: named `mounts` when
the mount table was non-empty, otherwise a single unscoped `filesystem` rooted
at `spec.basePath`. Both the fallback and the `/` root mount it guarded were
already unreachable — the only production caller (session-service →
buildAgentWorkspaceForRun) returns before the loader when `mountSpecs.length
=== 0`, and `omitRootMount` was hardcoded `true` at the single call site that
builds the spec. So the branch survived as a shape nothing selected but every
reader had to reason about.

It is also the wrong default to leave lying around: zero mounts silently yielded

commits.message:
fix(ai): name the "workspace declared but no mounts resolved" outcome

`resolveWorkspaceForRun` returned bare `undefined` when the resolved mount table
came back empty. It is the right decision — an agent whose every mount needed a
binding that isn't there (a `/task` mount on a session with no task, an
unsupported scope) should run without a workspace rather than with an empty one
— but it happened silently, and the consequence is not silent: the agent loses
its file and skill tools while its instructions still assume them. The symptom
reaches you as "the agent ignored its files", with nothing in the logs
connecting that to the mount table.

Now logged once with the agent, the run, and the declared mount paths that
failed to resolve, so the diagnosis is the log line instead of a bisect. Paired
with the loader's new zero-mount error: the loader refuses to build an
unscoped workspace, and this is the one caller allowed to decide "then none at
all" — out loud.

apps/ai 728 green; typecheck unchanged.

commits.message:
feat(ai): one containment resolver — the visibility chain reaches every run

Containment was implemented three times (WSP-01): resolveWorkContainer walked
DOWN for the artifact routes, the task-job specialist step hand-rolled the UP
walk for its file-tool prefixes, and the Mastra workspace mount table stopped
at the task tier entirely. The hand-rolled walk was also wrong: it never
consulted project_id, so a task inside a project never saw the project
workspace even though the tier and columns exist.

resolveWorkVisibility (work-scope/) is now the one UP walk: routine? → task →
goal? → project? → global, most-specific-first, filling missing links from the
containment edges (task → goal_id/project_id, goal → project_id) and degrading
to the provable tiers on lookup failure — global always present.

Consumers:
- The specialist step's 22-line prefix block becomes one resolver call.
  Behavior change, intended: headless task runs linked (directly or via their
  goal) to a project now see ai/workspace/projects/<id>/.
- The mount table gains goal/project scopes+sources; every preset mounts
  /goal and /project (rw for the whole chain — decision 2026-08-04),
  requireBinding so an unlinked chat run simply drops them. session-service
  resolves the chain right after task binding and feeds the mount context.
- resolveWorkContainer keeps the DOWN walk; both directions now live in
  work-scope/ and the headers say so.

Tests: 7 new resolver cases (ordering, both project-link paths, degradation,
no-lookup fast path), preset + scope-resolution pins updated. apps/ai 736
green, ai-core 4769 green, apps/core typecheck clean.

commits.message:
fix(invoices): normalize agent-written blocks through the shared canonical normalizer

TRK-07, part 1. The invoice/PDF "legacy vs new" line-item shapes are not an
old/new pair at all — both producers are live:

- the shared commercial editor writes `amount`/`cost_per_item`/`tax` and
  renders a phase as a `headline` block with `is_phase: true`;
- the invoices AI face was documented to write `quantity`/`unit_price`/
  `tax_rate` and a literal `type: "phase"`.

`invoices_replace_blocks` stored whatever it was given. The result is a real
defect, not just duplicate code: an agent-written line item renders as 0 in the
editor and in `calculateLineItemsSubtotal` (both read amount/cost_per_item),
and a `type: "phase"` block is dropped entirely by `groupBlocksForEditor`,
which knows no such type. Offers fixed this with `normalizeAgentBlock`;
invoices never got it and grew dual-branch readers instead.

Lift offers' normalizer into ONE implementation —
`@engenty/commercial-editor/blocks` (pure subpath, no React, so module server
code can import it) — and funnel invoices through it too. Offers behavior is
unchanged; its tests move with the function.

Invoice AI-face docs now name the canonical keys, matching the offers skill
wording that aliases are accepted and normalized.

`resolveWorkspaceForRun` returned bare `undefined` when the resolved mount table
came back empty. It is the right decision — an agent whose every mount needed a
binding that isn't there (a `/task` mount on a session with no task, an
unsupported scope) should run without a workspace rather than with an empty one
— but it happened silently, and the consequence is not silent: the agent loses
its file and skill tools while its instructions still assume them. The symptom
reaches you as "the agent ignored its files", with nothing in the logs
connecting that to the mount table.

failed to resolve, so the diagnosis is the log line instead of a bisect. Paired
with the loader's new zero-mount error: the loader refuses to build an
unscoped workspace, and this is the one caller allowed to decide "then none at
all" — out loud.

commits.message: one workspace shape — named mounts, no unscoped fallback
commits.body:
`createEngentyAgentWorkspace` built a Workspace two ways: named `mounts` when
the mount table was non-empty, otherwise a single unscoped `filesystem` rooted
at `spec.basePath`. Both the fallback and the `/` root mount it guarded were
already unreachable — the only production caller (session-service →
buildAgentWorkspaceForRun) returns before the loader when `mountSpecs.length
=== 0`, and `omitRootMount` was hardcoded `true` at the single call site that
builds the spec. So the branch survived as a shape nothing selected but every
reader had to reason about.

It is also the wrong default to leave lying around: zero mounts silently yielded
an agent a BROADER view than its declaration granted — one filesystem at the
tenant base path instead of the `/home`, `/skills`, `/shared`, `/task` it asked
for. A workspace IS its mount table, so zero mounts is now an error naming the
agent, not a fallback. The caller keeps deciding "no mounts → no workspace";
reaching the loader with none is a wiring bug and now says so.

Removed with it: `omitRootMount` (one value in production), `basePath` and the
three-way sandbox/home/tenant-root computation that fed it — both existed only
to construct the root filesystem. Sandbox staging paths are derived per mount
inside the loader and are unaffected.

The `Workspace` generic on the result stays bare deliberately: the chat path's
`placeholderSessionWorkspace` is a legitimately unmounted workspace, so the
conversation layer accepts both shapes and narrowing here would cascade into it.

footers.value:
the contracts test now asserts the refusal; two loader tests dropped the
removed fields. apps/ai 728 green; typecheck unchanged at its pre-existing 177.

commits.message: delete the unwired workspace-agent track and tool_profile
commits.body:
`assembleWorkspaceAgent` and `WorkspaceBackedAgentRegistry` were a second agent
assembly stack, built alongside the live one and never wired: zero callers, zero
production references, reachable only through two barrel re-exports. The live
path is `assembleDynamicAgent` over the composite `AiRegistry`. The "Module/core
tools still resolve through the optional legacy AiRegistry seam until W4" comment
lived in the dead copy, and `WorkspaceBackedAgentRegistry.getTool()` returning
undefined was that seam — in a provider no composite stack contains. There is no
W4 to schedule here, only a duplicate to remove.

`tool_profile` went with it. It was designed as a deny-by-default tool ceiling
"regardless of what is stored in the agent's config row", but all three legs are
missing: the only enforcement lived in the dead assembler, `ai.engenty_ai_agents`
has no `tool_profile` column so it cannot round-trip, and the one agent that
declared it (`knowledge-base.answers`) is a module agent served from code through
ModuleProvider and never persisted — so there is no stored row to clamp. Its
declared toolIds already equal the allowlist exactly. Reviving it means building
the column and the enforcement, which is different work from keeping the husk.

`tool-profiles.test.ts` stayed green because it reimplemented the filter in the
test rather than calling shipped code — the reason this went unnoticed. The
registrar test keeps the assertion that actually binds now (the answers agent
declares only the two scoped read tools) and says so.

footers.value:
assemble-workspace-agent.ts, workspace-agent-registry.ts,
tool-profiles.ts, tool-profiles.test.ts, agentToolProfileSchema/AgentToolProfile
and the tool_profile field from AgentConfig + the workspace contract.

no new typecheck errors (apps/ai's pre-existing debt unchanged).

commits.message:
fix(web-ingest)!: one SSRF guard, and validate every redirect hop

`isBlockedHostname` only ever looked at the literal hostname string, so a name
that merely RESOLVES to 169.254.169.254 or 10.x walked straight through it. It
was the sole guard on two server-side fetch paths — document-sources
(fetchText/fetchRawHtml/probeHttpMetadata) and knowledge-base media capture —
while the DNS-resolving `assertPublicHttpHost` guarded only web-ingest's own
adapter. Two tracks, and the weak one protected the exposed paths (TRK-01).

Both call sites now resolve the host, and `isBlockedHostname` is no longer
exported: it stays as the internal fast path of `assertPublicHttpHost`, so
there is one public guard and no way to look guarded without being guarded.

Validating the initial URL is not sufficient on its own — `fetch` defaults to
`redirect: "follow"`, so a public URL answering 302 lands wherever it likes.
The fetch-http adapter already followed redirects by hand, validating each hop;
that logic is now `safeFetchFollowingRedirects` in web-ingest, and all four
paths share it instead of the adapter owning the only correct copy.

`assertPublicHttpUrl` is async as a result; its 8 call sites now await it.

Tests: 9 new cases pin the hop validation (302 into link-local/RFC1918 is
refused and the blocked address is never requested, redirect:"manual" is always
set, a public-looking host that resolves private is refused before any fetch).
web-ingest 109 green, document-sources 31 green, both packages typecheck clean.

commits.message:
fix(engenty-coordinator)!: drop the orphaned pg_cron coordinator heartbeat

`private.trigger_coordinator_heartbeat` was the first of three generations of
the same job and outlived both successors (TRK-02):

  1. pg_cron 'engenty-coordinator-heartbeat' → this function → POST
     /ai/v1/conductor/run, authenticated from the 'conductor_service_jwt'
     Vault secret.
  2. 20260611180000 unscheduled that job and routed the heartbeat through
     private.trigger_engenty_routines_tick → POST /ai/v1/routines/tick. The
     function was kept only "until the routine cycle is verified live".
  3. 20260702000200 dropped the routines tick function outright; the heartbeat
     now runs as a scheduled Trigger on the apps/ai Mastra scheduler.

What survived was a SECURITY DEFINER function with no cron job pointing at it,
POSTing to a route apps/ai no longer serves, reading a Vault secret nothing can
mint since v0.1.93 deleted the static service JWT and mint-service-jwt.mjs.

Verified before dropping: no cron job and no vault secret in the dev DB, no
route matching /conductor/run or /routines/tick anywhere in apps/ai, and after
applying, zero pg_proc bodies reference conductor_service_jwt. Prod runs the
heartbeat as a Mastra-scheduled trigger (confirmed live 2026-08-04), so the
pg_cron path is dead there too; its Vault secret, if present, is now inert and
the migration header documents removing it by hand rather than deleting another
deployment's secret from a migration.

Also drops the config.toml.example claim that jwt_expiry is bumped "by
mint-service-jwt.mjs" — that script no longer exists, and the setting was never
related to service identity.

commits.message:
fix(approvals): one goal-grant implementation, and actually reap it

TRK-03. `core.agent_goal_grants` was the store D2 never folded, and it had
decayed into: two independent read implementations, a writer with no callers,
and a documented goal-end reap that nothing ever called.

Not folded into core.approval_grants, deliberately. They look alike and are
not: `approval_grants` records that an OPERATION was approved for a subject and
`consumeApprovalGrant` matches `operation_id` exactly, while goal grants record
that a CAPABILITY was elevated for the pursuit of a goal and are matched with
`capabilityCovers` — hierarchical and wildcard-aware. Putting capability
strings in an exact-match column would either break the match or invite loosening
it, which is how the capability sub-tree escalation trap gets re-opened. The
reasoning now lives at the top of the module instead of nowhere, so the second
table is a decision rather than an accident.

What changed:
- packages/approvals-sdk/goal-capability-grants.ts is the single implementation.
  apps/core's DAL is deleted and modules/secrets' inline copy (which existed only
  because modules cannot import apps/core — the same pressure that created every
  store this SDK exists to absorb) now calls it. Its test moved with it.
- `grantForGoal` deleted: zero callers. The secrets reveal path writes through
  `grantCapabilityForGoal`, keeping buildGoalGrantRow as the tested statement of
  the 24h TTL and the agent_id:null ("any agent on this goal") semantics.
- The reap is wired: goals_update into achieved/cancelled, and goals_delete,
  both call it through a `reapGoalGrants` seam on TasksGatewayOptions. Elevation
  no longer outlives the goal it was granted for; previously only expires_at
  bounded it, and rows written without one never lapsed. Best-effort by design —
  a failed reap must not roll back the goal transition, so it falls back to TTL.

Also drops the modules/tasks plugin comment claiming tool approvals dual-write
to task-row columns; those columns were dropped in 20260803210000 (TRK-12).

Tests: 6 new cases pin the reap (fires on achieved/cancelled and delete, does
not fire while planned/active, goal update survives a failing reap). core
typecheck 0, tasks typecheck 0, 134 tests green across tasks/approvals/secrets.

commits.message:
fix(ai): never open a live tool call with an empty name ("Ran tool")

Azure surfaces dynamic tools' input-streaming-start before the tool name
and Mastra passes that through as toolName "", so the live bridge opened
the AG-UI tool call nameless; the NAMED tool_start that followed was
deduped as already-started, and every workspace_action row in the chat
froze as the UI's "Ran tool" placeholder. The session bridge now holds
the START until a named event arrives (args always ride the full
tool_start), opening nameless-to-the-end calls under the explicit
placeholder so END/RESULT still pair up. Same empty-name hardening on
the durable replay bridge.

commits.message:
fix(core)!: delete deprecated route aliases — one leaked audit logs cross-tenant

TRK-06 plus TRK-04's dead half. Four routes were registered unconditionally
beside their successors, distinguished only by a `Deprecation: true` header.
Nothing outside tests called any of them; the UI has used the successors
throughout.

GET /api/security/audit was not merely redundant — it was a cross-tenant read.
It authorized with `requireAuth` (any principal resolves) and then took
`tenant_id` STRAIGHT FROM THE QUERY with no comparison to the caller's tenant,
and no default. So any authenticated user could read another tenant's audit log
by naming it, or omit the parameter and page through every tenant's events. Its
successor /api/security/audit/events uses `requireAuthForAudit`, defaults to the
caller's tenant, and 403s on mismatch — the fix already existed and shipped
next to the hole rather than replacing it. This is the concrete cost of keeping
a superseded path: the fix lands on the new route and the old one keeps serving.

Removed, with successors:
  GET  /api/modules/operations       → /api/operations/contracts
  POST /api/modules/ops/:operationId → /api/operations/:operationId/invoke
  POST /api/mcp/call/:operationId    → /api/mcp/tools/:operationId/call
  GET  /api/security/audit           → /api/security/audit/events

Tests migrated to the successors; the two that asserted deprecated behavior now
assert 404, so a reintroduction fails the suite. The audit one carries the
tenant-leak reasoning so it is not "cleaned up" back into existence.

Same commit finishes TRK-04's dead half: apps/core/src/lib/ai-config.ts is
deleted (all six exports had zero callers, including a four-deep
config→legacy-config→env→legacy-env model fallback chain), and the two docs that
described that chain as the live mechanism now describe the real one — model
role bindings seeded once from one env var per role. The nested legacy aliases
in ROLE_ENV_KEYS (AI_CLASSIFIER_MODEL behind router, AI_CODE_EXECUTION_MODEL
behind planning_coding) are gone, so a role's seed has exactly one source; prod
sets none of them, verified before removal.

apps/core typecheck 0, full apps/core suite 705 green.

old shape, which is a data-migration call rather than a deletion.

commits.message: delete deprecated route aliases — one leaked audit logs cross-tenant
commits.body:
TRK-06 plus TRK-04's dead half. Four routes were registered unconditionally
beside their successors, distinguished only by a `Deprecation: true` header.
Nothing outside tests called any of them; the UI has used the successors
throughout.

GET /api/security/audit was not merely redundant — it was a cross-tenant read.
It authorized with `requireAuth` (any principal resolves) and then took
`tenant_id` STRAIGHT FROM THE QUERY with no comparison to the caller's tenant,
and no default. So any authenticated user could read another tenant's audit log
by naming it, or omit the parameter and page through every tenant's events. Its
successor /api/security/audit/events uses `requireAuthForAudit`, defaults to the
caller's tenant, and 403s on mismatch — the fix already existed and shipped
next to the hole rather than replacing it. This is the concrete cost of keeping
a superseded path: the fix lands on the new route and the old one keeps serving.

Removed, with successors:
  GET  /api/modules/operations       → /api/operations/contracts
  POST /api/modules/ops/:operationId → /api/operations/:operationId/invoke
  POST /api/mcp/call/:operationId    → /api/mcp/tools/:operationId/call
  GET  /api/security/audit           → /api/security/audit/events

Tests migrated to the successors; the two that asserted deprecated behavior now
assert 404, so a reintroduction fails the suite. The audit one carries the
tenant-leak reasoning so it is not "cleaned up" back into existence.

Same commit finishes TRK-04's dead half: apps/core/src/lib/ai-config.ts is
deleted (all six exports had zero callers, including a four-deep
config→legacy-config→env→legacy-env model fallback chain), and the two docs that
described that chain as the live mechanism now describe the real one — model
role bindings seeded once from one env var per role. The nested legacy aliases
in ROLE_ENV_KEYS (AI_CLASSIFIER_MODEL behind router, AI_CODE_EXECUTION_MODEL
behind planning_coding) are gone, so a role's seed has exactly one source; prod
sets none of them, verified before removal.

apps/core typecheck 0, full apps/core suite 705 green.

commits.message: never open a live tool call with an empty name ("Ran tool")
commits.body:
Azure surfaces dynamic tools' input-streaming-start before the tool name
and Mastra passes that through as toolName "", so the live bridge opened
the AG-UI tool call nameless; the NAMED tool_start that followed was
deduped as already-started, and every workspace_action row in the chat
froze as the UI's "Ran tool" placeholder. The session bridge now holds
the START until a named event arrives (args always ride the full
tool_start), opening nameless-to-the-end calls under the explicit
placeholder so END/RESULT still pair up. Same empty-name hardening on
the durable replay bridge.

commits.message: one goal-grant implementation, and actually reap it
commits.body:
TRK-03. `core.agent_goal_grants` was the store D2 never folded, and it had
decayed into: two independent read implementations, a writer with no callers,
and a documented goal-end reap that nothing ever called.

Not folded into core.approval_grants, deliberately. They look alike and are
not: `approval_grants` records that an OPERATION was approved for a subject and
`consumeApprovalGrant` matches `operation_id` exactly, while goal grants record
that a CAPABILITY was elevated for the pursuit of a goal and are matched with
`capabilityCovers` — hierarchical and wildcard-aware. Putting capability
strings in an exact-match column would either break the match or invite loosening
it, which is how the capability sub-tree escalation trap gets re-opened. The
reasoning now lives at the top of the module instead of nowhere, so the second
table is a decision rather than an accident.

What changed:
- packages/approvals-sdk/goal-capability-grants.ts is the single implementation.
  apps/core's DAL is deleted and modules/secrets' inline copy (which existed only
  because modules cannot import apps/core — the same pressure that created every
  store this SDK exists to absorb) now calls it. Its test moved with it.
- `grantForGoal` deleted: zero callers. The secrets reveal path writes through
  `grantCapabilityForGoal`, keeping buildGoalGrantRow as the tested statement of
  the 24h TTL and the agent_id:null ("any agent on this goal") semantics.
- The reap is wired: goals_update into achieved/cancelled, and goals_delete,
  both call it through a `reapGoalGrants` seam on TasksGatewayOptions. Elevation
  no longer outlives the goal it was granted for; previously only expires_at
  bounded it, and rows written without one never lapsed. Best-effort by design —
  a failed reap must not roll back the goal transition, so it falls back to TTL.

Also drops the modules/tasks plugin comment claiming tool approvals dual-write
to task-row columns; those columns were dropped in 20260803210000 (TRK-12).

footers.value:
6 new cases pin the reap (fires on achieved/cancelled and delete, does
not fire while planned/active, goal update survives a failing reap). core
typecheck 0, tasks typecheck 0, 134 tests green across tasks/approvals/secrets.

commits.message: drop the orphaned pg_cron coordinator heartbeat
commits.body:
`private.trigger_coordinator_heartbeat` was the first of three generations of
the same job and outlived both successors (TRK-02):

  1. pg_cron 'engenty-coordinator-heartbeat' → this function → POST
     /ai/v1/conductor/run, authenticated from the 'conductor_service_jwt'
     Vault secret.
  2. 20260611180000 unscheduled that job and routed the heartbeat through
     private.trigger_engenty_routines_tick → POST /ai/v1/routines/tick. The
     function was kept only "until the routine cycle is verified live".
  3. 20260702000200 dropped the routines tick function outright; the heartbeat
     now runs as a scheduled Trigger on the apps/ai Mastra scheduler.

What survived was a SECURITY DEFINER function with no cron job pointing at it,
POSTing to a route apps/ai no longer serves, reading a Vault secret nothing can
mint since v0.1.93 deleted the static service JWT and mint-service-jwt.mjs.

Verified before dropping: no cron job and no vault secret in the dev DB, no
route matching /conductor/run or /routines/tick anywhere in apps/ai, and after
applying, zero pg_proc bodies reference conductor_service_jwt. Prod runs the
heartbeat as a Mastra-scheduled trigger (confirmed live 2026-08-04), so the
pg_cron path is dead there too; its Vault secret, if present, is now inert and
the migration header documents removing it by hand rather than deleting another
deployment's secret from a migration.

Also drops the config.toml.example claim that jwt_expiry is bumped "by
mint-service-jwt.mjs" — that script no longer exists, and the setting was never
related to service identity.

commits.message: one SSRF guard, and validate every redirect hop
commits.body:
`isBlockedHostname` only ever looked at the literal hostname string, so a name
that merely RESOLVES to 169.254.169.254 or 10.x walked straight through it. It
was the sole guard on two server-side fetch paths — document-sources
(fetchText/fetchRawHtml/probeHttpMetadata) and knowledge-base media capture —
while the DNS-resolving `assertPublicHttpHost` guarded only web-ingest's own
adapter. Two tracks, and the weak one protected the exposed paths (TRK-01).

Both call sites now resolve the host, and `isBlockedHostname` is no longer
exported: it stays as the internal fast path of `assertPublicHttpHost`, so
there is one public guard and no way to look guarded without being guarded.

Validating the initial URL is not sufficient on its own — `fetch` defaults to
`redirect: "follow"`, so a public URL answering 302 lands wherever it likes.
The fetch-http adapter already followed redirects by hand, validating each hop;
that logic is now `safeFetchFollowingRedirects` in web-ingest, and all four
paths share it instead of the adapter owning the only correct copy.

`assertPublicHttpUrl` is async as a result; its 8 call sites now await it.

footers.value:
9 new cases pin the hop validation (302 into link-local/RFC1918 is
refused and the blocked address is never requested, redirect:"manual" is always
set, a public-looking host that resolves private is refused before any fetch).
web-ingest 109 green, document-sources 31 green, both packages typecheck clean.

commits.message:
fix(remote): channel approval policy "request" — defer executed gated ops

The overnight approval saga, third and final act. "suspend" rendered no card
and parked in-process (no tool-call-approval chunk). "defer" — the first
replacement — turned out to be an unattended-execution hole: it skips the
AI-side pre-gate and trusts core, but the delegated actor token makes the
channel principal the USER, and core has never gated user principals (the
web-chat Approve card is the AI-side pre-gate's UX, not a core gate). Live
result: a Slack DM created a high-risk requiresApproval contact with no
approval. Agent attribution (agentTypeKey/agentId now set on the ALS scope —
kept, it is correct for audit and agent-aware core gates like the secrets
reveal) did not change core's decision.

"request" runs the pre-gate and returns a structured approval_pending
WITHOUT executing. Verified live against the dev stack: contacts_create
answered approval_pending in 213ms, zero rows created, and the turn ended
with an honest reply instead of a spinning card.

commits.message:
fix(ai): say it loudly when the scheduler serves only part of the platform

A tenant-bound service credential is a valid least-privilege configuration
while an install has ONE tenant. The moment it has more, the foreign mints
are refused and those tenants' triggers and system jobs silently never
fire — the per-tenant warns scroll away and nothing else says the platform
is half-served.

Report it once, at error level, naming the skipped tenants and the remedy
(re-mint platform-scoped). Still non-fatal: the tenants that CAN be served
keep running rather than taking the whole scheduler down with them.

commits.message:
refactor(ai)!: delete the userAccessToken scope shim, rename bags to accessToken

The AiSessionScope shim kept scope literals compiling through the CP4→CP6
window; with CP6 executed it is gone — `credential` (the kind-tagged union)
is the only way a scope carries a bearer, so every literal now states
whether it is a user or a service principal. resolveScopeCredential loses
its legacy branch.

The option bags CP4 left named userAccessToken — EngentyCoreClientOptions,
AppCapabilityGrant, ExternalChannelDispatchScope, EngentyToolsRunContext,
and the workspace/vault client options — are renamed to accessToken: they
carry whatever bearer the scope resolved, not specifically a user's.

Also pins down two sites the compiler could not see (as-never / as-cast
scope literals in app-proxy-routes.test.ts and app-build-steps.ts) and
fixes 10 pre-existing tenantRole-widening tsc errors in touched test files
(apps/ai backlog 190 → 180, zero new).

Repo grep for userAccessToken: empty. 730 apps/ai tests green.

commits.message: say it loudly when the scheduler serves only part of the platform
commits.body:
A tenant-bound service credential is a valid least-privilege configuration
while an install has ONE tenant. The moment it has more, the foreign mints
are refused and those tenants' triggers and system jobs silently never
fire — the per-tenant warns scroll away and nothing else says the platform
is half-served.

Report it once, at error level, naming the skipped tenants and the remedy
(re-mint platform-scoped). Still non-fatal: the tenants that CAN be served
keep running rather than taking the whole scheduler down with them.

commits.message: channel approval policy "request" — defer executed gated ops
commits.body:
The overnight approval saga, third and final act. "suspend" rendered no card
and parked in-process (no tool-call-approval chunk). "defer" — the first
replacement — turned out to be an unattended-execution hole: it skips the
AI-side pre-gate and trusts core, but the delegated actor token makes the
channel principal the USER, and core has never gated user principals (the
web-chat Approve card is the AI-side pre-gate's UX, not a core gate). Live
result: a Slack DM created a high-risk requiresApproval contact with no
approval. Agent attribution (agentTypeKey/agentId now set on the ALS scope —
kept, it is correct for audit and agent-aware core gates like the secrets
reveal) did not change core's decision.

"request" runs the pre-gate and returns a structured approval_pending
WITHOUT executing. Verified live against the dev stack: contacts_create
answered approval_pending in 213ms, zero rows created, and the turn ended
with an honest reply instead of a spinning card.

commits.message:
fix(remote): forward the workspace anchor so bindings route by workspace

The gate never sent external_workspace_id: resolveBindingForEvent is
workspace-first with a refuse-on-ambiguity fallback, but without the value a
workspace-anchored binding could never match — one anchor-less binding per
platform was the ceiling, and a second tenant binding Slack made events
unroutable. Now the gate extracts the anchor from the platform raw payload
(Slack: team_id / team string / team.id object / user.team_id — the shapes
Chat SDK itself documents; Telegram: none, the bot token is the anchor until
R4) and forwards it.

Live-verified against the dev stack with the binding anchored to a workspace:
a matching-team DM routed and provisioned its thread; a foreign-team DM was
refused with "no active binding" and wrote nothing.

commits.message:
feat(core,ai): platform-scoped service credential — multi-tenant headless plane

The headless plane (task dispatch, scheduled fires, remote actor mints)
ran as ONE tenant-bound service principal: any task dispatched for a
second tenant died on the tenant assertion. Now:

- core.service_credential.tenant_id is nullable; NULL = platform-scoped.
  The exchange takes an explicit tenantId per mint — the minted token is
  ALWAYS tenant-scoped (this widens where a token can be minted for,
  never what any one token can do). Tenant-bound credentials 403 foreign
  requests; platform mints verify the tenant exists; audit carries
  platformScoped + the minted tenant.
- apps/ai vends per-tenant service tokens (per-tenant session cache).
  An explicit tenant request now beats the static ENGENTY_AI_SERVICE_JWT
  when the durable secret is configured — a static JWT is single-tenant
  by construction and silently degraded the whole plane back to one
  tenant.
- Task dispatch mints for the message's tenant; the loud tenant
  assertion stays as the belt.
- Scheduler enumerates core.tenants and reconciles/fires per tenant; a
  tenant whose scope cannot be minted is skipped, not fatal.
- Remote channels mint actor tokens per binding tenant; sender
  resolution runs under the installation's first tenant as a marked
  interim until the remote track grows a platform lane.

E2E: dev credential flipped to platform scope; a Goals-Test-tenant task
checked out 1s after dispatch with per-tenant mints for all 3 tenants.

commits.message:
feat(remote): honest channel approvals (defer), conversations UI, housekeeping

Approvals through a channel turn, tested live with the stub Slack: the gate's
approvalPolicy "suspend" — commented "(Phase 3)" — renders NO Approve/Deny
card. Chat SDK's driver renders buttons only on Mastra's native
tool-call-approval chunk; the engenty approval suspends from inside the tool
(workflow suspension), which never emits it, so the Slack user stares at a
spinning tool card while the run parks in the in-process 15-min map with no
resume path from Slack. Channel turns now use "defer": core (the
authoritative policy engine) records a durable approval request, the tool
returns approval_pending, the turn ends with a real reply, and the inbox
pings a human — aligned with the D2 unified-approvals direction. In-place
cards + resume = ride Mastra's native tool-approval flow, built on top of D2.

Conversations become visible: the copilot drawer filters by agent id, so
engenty.remote threads appeared nowhere — new remote_conversations_list op +
a Conversations section on the module settings page (platform thread,
DM/channel, backing engenty thread, last activity).

Housekeeping: inbound_events now prunes 7d-old rows opportunistically on the
ingest path (non-fatal, no scheduler dependency); REMOTE_PLATFORMS aligned to
the provider registry (slack, telegram — whatsapp/teams dropped, they never
had an adapter); docs updated with the routing-table model, chat controls,
SLACK_API_URL testing, a real-workspace E2E runbook, and a first-prod-
enablement checklist.

commits.message:
fix(ai): close the tenant-readiness gaps behind the per-tenant scheduler

A dedicated multi-tenant sweep after fa6ba5c61 found the headless plane
still leaning on single-tenant assumptions — two of them destructive
once every tenant reconciles:

- reconcileScheduler's orphan sweep ran over the GLOBAL Mastra schedule
  store: with N tenants reconciling, each pass deleted every other
  tenant's schedules (last tenant wins, all other tenants' triggers
  silently stop firing). Sweep is now scoped to the reconciling tenant.
- System-job schedule ids were not tenant-qualified — the first tenant
  to reconcile claimed hb_system-<job> and no other tenant ever got
  inbox sync / calendar sync. Ids are now hb_system-<tenant>-<job>;
  legacy rows are cleaned by the (now scoped) orphan sweep.
- POST /triggers/reconcile invoked with a tenant-less service token:
  400s outright on a platform credential and creates/lists trigger rows
  in the credential's tenant otherwise. Now minted for the caller's
  tenant.
- Team-chat mention consumer read threads and posted replies on a
  tenant-less token; now minted for the dispatch tenant.
- Email notifier was single-tenant by construction (one resolved
  service tenant, foreign records skipped forever). The cross-tenant
  scan now groups by the tenant in the thread id and sends each batch
  on that tenant's invoker; an unservable tenant stays pending.
- Remote channels: the resolveSender interim (first-tenant) invoker
  leaked into thread provisioning and chat controls; those now ride the
  binding tenant. The interim is confined to resolveSender itself.
- createSchedulerOperationInvoker now ASSERTS the minted token's tenant
  (memoized per token) — a static ENGENTY_AI_SERVICE_JWT or password
  grant can no longer execute tenant B's operation inside tenant A
  silently; same belt the task-job path wears.

Not addressed here (tracked): remote_outbound single-bot delivery →
R4 per-tenant credentials spec; tenant list captured once at boot;
SDK mapping threads keyed without tenant.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message: platform-scoped service credential — multi-tenant headless plane
commits.body:
The headless plane (task dispatch, scheduled fires, remote actor mints)
ran as ONE tenant-bound service principal: any task dispatched for a
second tenant died on the tenant assertion. Now:

- core.service_credential.tenant_id is nullable; NULL = platform-scoped.
  The exchange takes an explicit tenantId per mint — the minted token is
  ALWAYS tenant-scoped (this widens where a token can be minted for,
  never what any one token can do). Tenant-bound credentials 403 foreign
  requests; platform mints verify the tenant exists; audit carries
  platformScoped + the minted tenant.
- apps/ai vends per-tenant service tokens (per-tenant session cache).
  An explicit tenant request now beats the static ENGENTY_AI_SERVICE_JWT
  when the durable secret is configured — a static JWT is single-tenant
  by construction and silently degraded the whole plane back to one
  tenant.
- Task dispatch mints for the message's tenant; the loud tenant
  assertion stays as the belt.
- Scheduler enumerates core.tenants and reconciles/fires per tenant; a
  tenant whose scope cannot be minted is skipped, not fatal.
- Remote channels mint actor tokens per binding tenant; sender
  resolution runs under the installation's first tenant as a marked
  interim until the remote track grows a platform lane.

footers.value:
dev credential flipped to platform scope; a Goals-Test-tenant task
checked out 1s after dispatch with per-tenant mints for all 3 tenants.

commits.message: forward the workspace anchor so bindings route by workspace
commits.body:
The gate never sent external_workspace_id: resolveBindingForEvent is
workspace-first with a refuse-on-ambiguity fallback, but without the value a
workspace-anchored binding could never match — one anchor-less binding per
platform was the ceiling, and a second tenant binding Slack made events
unroutable. Now the gate extracts the anchor from the platform raw payload
(Slack: team_id / team string / team.id object / user.team_id — the shapes
Chat SDK itself documents; Telegram: none, the bot token is the anchor until
R4) and forwards it.

Live-verified against the dev stack with the binding anchored to a workspace:
a matching-team DM routed and provisioned its thread; a foreign-team DM was
refused with "no active binding" and wrote nothing.

commits.message:
fix(remote): return tenant_id from resolve_sender; SLACK_API_URL test seam

Found by the R2 live spike: bindingShape had no tenant_id, and zod strips
unknown keys, so the resolve op silently dropped the one field the channel
runtime derives its whole turn scope from — actor-token mints went out with
tenant_id "" and core answered 400. Every mapped-sender unit test passed
throughout, because they stub the raw HTTP response and never cross the
module-side schema. The fix is one schema field; the lesson is recorded in
the plan.

SLACK_API_URL (dev/E2E only) points the Slack adapter at a stub Web API so a
full turn can run without a real workspace — this is what let the spike drive
webhook → gate → provisioning → model turn → tenant-scoped persistence
end-to-end against the dev stack. Spike results + the adapter-post
crash-hardening finding are in PLAN-remote-channels-consolidation.md.

commits.message:
fix(ai): survive adapter-post failures in the channel render driver

Chat SDK creates driverPromise with a rethrowing .catch and only awaits it at
the terminal stream chunk; a driver that fails EARLY (first chat.postMessage —
bad token, or a Slack outage) rejects in that window with no owner, and Node
kills the whole apps/ai process. Observed live in the R2 spike: one failing
Slack post took down the runtime for every tenant.

Two layers:
- patches/@mastra__core@1.52.1.patch — attach a no-op catch branch to
  driverPromise so the rejection is owned; the terminal await still observes
  it and logs "channel render driver failed". Revisit on any Mastra upgrade.
- process-level unhandledRejection guard in apps/ai/src/index.ts that logs
  loudly instead of crashing — this process hosts every tenant's agent
  runtime, and dependency async work does escape ownership. uncaughtException
  is deliberately untouched: a synchronous throw means unknown state and the
  default crash-and-supervise remains correct.

Verified by rerunning the exact crash scenario (dummy Slack token, real Slack
API): adapter failures logged ("failed early" from the patch's owned path,
then "failed" at the terminal await), health endpoint alive after the turn,
zero crash banners. The guard itself never fired — the patch catches it at
the root; the guard is defense-in-depth.

commits.message:
fix(core,ai,modules): keep service-principal ids out of user columns

A headless run acts as the AI service principal, whose `principalId` is a
core.service_credential id — not a core.users row. Handlers were writing it
straight into attribution columns that carry a foreign key to core.users, so
the insert either failed the constraint or recorded a user that does not exist.

`PluginAuthContext` now carries `principalType`, plumbed from the operation
routes, and `actorUserIdFromAuth()` reads it: the principal id for a user,
null for anything else. Absent means "user" — the assumption every caller made
before service principals existed — so nothing that already worked changes.

Converted the attribution sites in tasks, triggers, offers, secrets,
knowledge-base, connections and team-hr, and the apps/ai thread/run path:
`scopeAttributionUserId` on the session scope, a nullable `createdByUserId`
through the session store and run tracker, and no `thread_participant` owner
row for a service-created thread (its principal types only cover users and
groups). The migration drops `not null` from `ai.thread.created_by_user_id`,
matching `ai.agent_run.created_by_user_id`, which has been nullable all along
— code and migration must land together or the write fails.

Triggers were the one path still writing the id raw, and the one that matters
most: `created_by_user_id` is a core.users FK on both the trigger row and every
task it materializes, and the scheduler drives exactly that path as the service
principal. Tests pin the attribution for both principal kinds there, so a
revert fails in CI rather than silently in prod.

commits.message:
feat(copilot): give the supervisor app_build instead of only delegation

The copilot was delegation-only for app requests: build a tool, a form, a
calculator, and it was meant to hand off to engenty.app-coder. Two live runs
showed it doing something else — scaffolding files into its own workspace and
calling that an app. Nothing a user can run is ever produced there, so the
request quietly fails while looking like it succeeded.

Delegation being the only correct path made dodging it the path of least
resistance. So the correct path is now in the supervisor's own tool belt:
`app_build` is one call that creates the app, compiles it, and publishes the
live preview into the chat. Delegation remains the route for larger, iterative
builds, and AGENTS.md draws that line explicitly — along with naming the dead
ends (own-workspace files, raw catalog operations, engenty_cli, and answering
with a document that merely contains the code).

The wiring test asserts both halves: `app_build` in ENGENTY_COPILOT_TOOL_IDS
and resolvable in the builtin registry. If either drops, the dodge returns
silently.

commits.message:
fix(ci): make the turbo remote cache actually cache

The remote cache has been deployed and configured all along
(build-cache.engrd.xyz, TURBO_API/TURBO_TEAM/TURBO_TOKEN set), and it has been
doing almost nothing. Two independent reasons, both silent.

Uploads were timing out. turbo's default upload timeout is 60s and the largest
module artifacts — a dist/ carrying bundled .d.ts — do not finish in that. A
timed-out upload is only a WARNING:

  the cache artifact for 2a67b8ffe2730aef was too large to upload within the timeout

so the build goes green while the artifact is never written, and every later run
misses that task again, forever. Five artifacts hit this on v0.1.89 alone. Both
workflows now set TURBO_REMOTE_CACHE_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT=300.

And publish-packages.yml had no local turbo cache at all — it was the one job
without the actions/cache restore/save that ci.yml has carried since v0.1.40. On
v0.1.89 it ran 0 cache hits against 70 misses and took 26 minutes, overrunning
its 30-minute job timeout and cancelling the release's package publish. It now
restores under the same `turbo-<os>-` prefix ci.yml saves to, so it starts from
whatever main last built (a tag run may read the default branch's caches), and
saves under a `-modules` suffix so it seeds the next release without colliding
with ci.yml's immutable keys.

Worth knowing for next time: the deploy was never the missing piece. The cache
server was up, "Remote caching enabled" was printed on every run, and the thing
was still empty — because the only symptom of a failed write is a warning
nobody reads. Documented in docs/content/dev/ci-pipeline.md with the string to
grep for.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(core): make approvals durable — one store for requests and grants

Core's approval requests and the grants they produced lived in a per-process
Map, so a restart lost every pending request and every standing "allow" a
human had already given, and a second replica never saw the first one's. This
is the D2 consolidation's first slice: core.approval_requests +
core.approval_grants, generalizing the tasks module's proven approval_grants
columns into core where evaluatePolicy can reach them.

Requests and grants are separate tables deliberately — a request is audit
history worth keeping after the fact, a grant is live authorization that gets
consumed, and collapsing them would make deleting a used grant destroy the
record. The scope enum already carries task/trigger/goal so the tasks-module
and agent_goal_grants writers can fold in later without another migration.

Two pre-existing bugs fall out on the way:
- listPending() had NO tenant filter; /api/security/approvals pulled every
  tenant's queue and narrowed it in JS afterwards. The filter is now the
  store's, and the cross-tenant superadmin queue is a separately named method
  so it cannot be reached by omitting an argument.
- decide() had no race guard, so two approvers both minted a grant. The update
  is conditioned on status = 'pending'; the loser reads back the decided row.

Tasks columns and agent_goal_grants keep their own stores this pass.

commits.message:
fix(core): bound and reap approval grants now that they outlive the process

The in-memory Map this store replaced was garbage-collected by process death,
which quietly bounded every grant it held. Durability removed that: an
"allow once" whose retry never came, or a session grant whose owner closed the
tab, would have sat in the table forever.

Grants that are not standing authorization now carry their own end (once: 1h,
session: 24h; policy keeps none, which is what standing means), and revoking a
session's token drops that session's grants immediately — logging out has to

commits.message:
refactor(core): one approval gate for all three transports

The `require_approval` branch was written out three times — invoke,
module-ops, and plugin HTTP — and the copies had drifted. The plugin-HTTP
one never recorded `policy.require_approval` and never returned
`expiresAt`, so the same blocked call produced a different audit trail and
a less useful 202 depending on which door it came through.

`applyApprovalGate` is now the single place a policy decision becomes
either "proceed" or "ask a human". Each call site keeps only its own
transport shape. Folding the remaining approval stores into this one is a
change to a single gate rather than three.

commits.message:
fix(secrets): stop in-chat secret grants from outliving their goal

`core.agent_goal_grants` rows were written with no expiry, and the DAL's
`revokeGoalGrants` — the reaper its own doc comment promises — has no
caller. So "yes, this agent may read that secret, for this conversation"
actually authorized every future agent on that goal, forever.

Grants now lapse after 24h. A lapsed grant re-gates the reveal and asks the
human again, which is how a secret grant should fail. The upsert no longer
ignores duplicates: with an expiry, a second approval has to renew the row
rather than skip the write and leave the human re-asked in a loop.

Reaping on goal completion is still the better fix and still owed — the
tasks module emits no event on a goal reaching a terminal status.

commits.message:
fix(remote): mount channel webhooks under /ai so they ride the core gateway

Mastra's getWebhookRoutes() emits paths shaped for Mastra's own server
(/api/agents/…/webhook) and they were mounted verbatim on the apps/ai
Hono app. Unprefixed, the path is shadowed by core's /api/* gateway rule
— the documented gateway URL 404'd, and the webhook only worked in dev
by exposing apps/ai directly, breaking the 'apps/ai is only reachable
via the core gateway' invariant (apps/ai holds the service credential,
the Docker socket, and the sandbox mount; it must not be internet-facing).

Prefix the mount with AI_BASE_PATH so /ai/api/agents/…/webhook resolves
through the gateway's /ai proxy like every other apps/ai route; add a
regression guard that the raw Mastra path stays unmounted; point the dev
tunnel instructions at the gateway origin.

commits.message:
feat(connections,core): fold connections approvals into the core store

The connections approval ledger (module_connections.approval_requests) was
request-only: approving a row set status='approved', emitted an event
nobody subscribed to, and unblocked nothing — the retried run filed a
fresh request and threw connection_approval_pending again. Only
grant_always changed the outcome. "Allow once" was a button that closed a
row.

Now there is one ledger and approvals actually approve:

- @engenty/approvals-sdk carries the core approval store client
  (moved from apps/core), so modules reach it without importing core.
- The connections profile policy attaches its connection context to the
  require_approval decision (new PolicyDecision.approvalContext); core's
  applyApprovalGate stores it on the ONE deduped request it files in
  core.approval_requests and emits a platform-wide `approval.requested`
  core event — replacing the module's own request write + event, which
  fired even when a grant let the call through.
- Deciding goes through the approval service: approve mints a one-shot
  core grant for the requesting principal. Both gates consume it — core's
  applyApprovalGate (already did) and now the connections-sdk executor's
  inner gate, which used to throw unconditionally.
- The owner check runs BEFORE the decide; it used to run after, so a
  non-owner's attempt burned the request and left the owner nothing to
  approve.
- The tasks module subscribes to connections.approval.decided (payload
  now carries task_id + operation_id) and resumes a task-linked blocked
  task via the existing v0.1.66 grant + re-dispatch flow.
- Migration carries still-pending rows into core; the old table stays as
  a read-only archive until a later drop.

Request TTL moves from 5 minutes to 7 days: these rows feed a durable
queue a person may open tomorrow morning, not a caller blocking on the
answer.

Smoke-verified against the dev DB end to end (request → list → decide →
grant → consume-once → race + cross-actor refusals): 11/11.

commits.message:
fix(remote): authorize the destination of proactive sends

remote_notify took external_thread_id from its caller — for an agent that
means model output — and validated only its shape. The consumer then
parsed tenant_id and never used it, posting wherever it was told via the
platform-level bot token. module_remote.conversations(tenant_id,
external_thread_id) already records exactly which threads a tenant has
conversed in; it was simply never consulted.

Any principal with module.engenty-remote.write (including a headless
agent) could therefore post up to 4000 chars into any thread the bot can
reach — cross-tenant message injection, and an exfiltration primitive for
an agent that can read tenant data.

Gate the send on findTenantConversation() at the operation, where the auth
context lives, and carry binding_id onto the queue. The consumer now
requires binding_id, so a payload that never passed the check — a pre-fix
message still queued, or a write that bypassed the op — is refused on the
far side of the process boundary.

Also enable the remote-channel runtime by default (manifest defaultValue),
and hydrate ENGENTY_REMOTE_CHANNELS_ENABLED from platform settings: the key
is platform-configurable so the Setup UI offers it, but it was absent from
the hydration list, so toggling it there silently did nothing.

commits.message:
refactor(remote): enable channels by opt-out, delete legacy channel cluster

Configuring a platform is now what turns the remote channel runtime on —
SLACK_BOT_TOKEN/SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET and TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN are declared by no
other feature, so their presence is an unambiguous signal of intent, and the
separate opt-in was redundant with the credential guard that already ran.
ENGENTY_REMOTE_CHANNELS_ENABLED=false remains as the kill switch, for shutting
ingress off during an incident without rotating or deleting a bot token.

Two consequences handled: the "no platform configured" branch is now the normal
state of every deployment that doesn't use remote channels, so it returns
silently instead of warning; and the outbound queue consumer keys on the runtime
having actually registered rather than on the switch, so a process with no live
Chat SDK leaves messages queued instead of failing every one.

Also deletes the legacy external-channel cluster (ai/channels.ts,
channel-interactions.ts, channel-outbound.ts, ~700 lines). Its routes were
removed in the 2026-06-20 cutover; what remained was config parsing and outbound
helpers reachable only through re-exports in ai/index.ts, with nothing calling
them. Removing it also retires a third Slack env convention (ENGENTY_AI_SLACK_*,
ENGENTY_AI_DISCORD_*, ENGENTY_AI_CHANNEL*), read nowhere else.

commits.message:
feat(core,tasks): task approvals mint core grants the gates can spend (D2 2c)

A task tool approval now writes two things: the task-row string[] columns
(unchanged — the run transport the AI pre-gate reads) and a durable row in
core.approval_grants, which is what core-side gates actually consume. Until
now "approve" from the task UI only satisfied the pre-gate; any core-level
gate (the connections profile policy foremost) 202'd the retry and filed a
second request nobody connected to the first.

Two grant axes become optional, mirroring agent_goal_grants.agent_id:
- actor_id NULL: the approval names the WORK, not the worker — decided
  before the retry's principal exists.
- module_id NULL: the approval names the OPERATION; operation ids are
  globally unique, so the module adds provenance, not precision.
Either agnostic axis requires a subject (DB check + writer + reader), so a
blank check cannot be minted or honored.

Backfill migration carries pre-dual-write approvals into the core store,
guarded for installs without the tasks module. The connections resume path
deliberately does NOT dual-write — decide already minted the core grant.
