commits.message:
feat(core,tasks,ai): dispatch reads approval grants from the core store (D2 2d)

The run's pre-gate grant set now comes from one place. buildBriefStep asks
the tasks module for the task's effective grants (new op
tasks_approval_grants_effective = core grants for the task+trigger subjects
∪ the trigger's approval_grants CONFIG — a routine's definition, not an
approval artifact) instead of merging the task-row columns itself. A failed
read grants nothing: the op gates again rather than running unapproved.

Once-grant lifecycle moves with it: core once-rows deliberately outlive
dispatch so a core-side gate can spend them DURING the run (deleting them at
dispatch would have broken the connections resume this store exists for);
the write-result step now reaps whatever the run didn't spend, with the same
best-effort tolerance the old dispatch-time column clear had.

x-engenty-trigger-id joins the task lane end to end (run context → client →
PrincipalContext → gate subjects), so routine-scoped grants are spendable at
core gates too, not only in the pre-gate transport.

The legacy task-row columns are still dual-written for rollback but no
longer read anywhere; dropping them is a follow-up release.

commits.message:
feat(core): evaluatePolicy spends approval grants itself (D2 phase 3)

A standing or subject-bound approval is authorization state exactly like a
capability, so the policy engine consults it during evaluation instead of
every transport pairing a require_approval result with its own
consume-then-request sequence. evaluatePolicy takes the approval service as
an optional dep, spends a covering grant (subjects = task/trigger/goal from
the principal context) and returns 'allow: approval grant'; a
require_approval that reaches a transport now always means a human has to
answer, and the transport's only job is fileApprovalRequest (the renamed,
consume-free applyApprovalGate) + 202.

reason 'approval grant' instead of the escalation reason.

commits.message:
feat(remote): routing table, dedicated tenant threads, chat controls (R1-R3)

R1 — the conversations routing table is now WRITTEN: resolve_sender upserts
the (binding, external_thread_id) row on every inbound event and records the
platform event id in inbound_events (durable dedup — Chat SDK's is in-memory
by design, so a restart inside a platform's retry window meant double
replies). This makes the ddbcf6be0 destination gate functional: previously it
read a table nothing wrote and failed closed on every proactive send.

R2 — one platform thread = one dedicated engenty thread on engenty.remote.
The identity gate pre-creates the SDK's mapping thread with our own UUID and
the exact metadata AgentChannels#getOrCreateThread filters on, so the SDK
adopts our thread id; the agent's memory is a per-turn resolver bound to the
ALS tenant scope, so channel messages persist through
EngentySessionMemoryStorage into ai.thread/ai.thread_message like every other
conversation. Never mixed with copilot threads.

R3 — chat controls parsed in the gate before the agent: /new (fresh thread),
/threads (list), /link <id> (the only sanctioned attach to a non-remote
thread — explicit, user-typed, ownership-checked), /help. Only exact tokens
are commands; unknown /words pass through.

Also (decision: platform validity is code, never a DB enum): providers get a
one-file-per-platform layout (api/remote-channels/providers/{slack,telegram})
behind RemoteChannelProvider {id, isConfigured, createAdapter}, and migration
20260803213500 drops the platform check constraints (they allowed
whatsapp/teams with no adapter and forbade discord).

Unit-tested (module 14, apps/ai 730 incl. replay-drop + command-parse + upsert
contract). NOT live-verified: the R2 spike (one real DM turn) and the Slack
E2E remain owed; R4 (per-tenant credentials via ChannelProvider) not started.

commits.message: evaluatePolicy spends approval grants itself (D2 phase 3)
commits.body:
A standing or subject-bound approval is authorization state exactly like a
capability, so the policy engine consults it during evaluation instead of
every transport pairing a require_approval result with its own
consume-then-request sequence. evaluatePolicy takes the approval service as
an optional dep, spends a covering grant (subjects = task/trigger/goal from
the principal context) and returns 'allow: approval grant'; a
require_approval that reaches a transport now always means a human has to
answer, and the transport's only job is fileApprovalRequest (the renamed,
consume-free applyApprovalGate) + 202.

Audit side effect: a grant-admitted call now records policy.allow with
reason 'approval grant' instead of the escalation reason.

commits.message: dispatch reads approval grants from the core store (D2 2d)
commits.body:
The run's pre-gate grant set now comes from one place. buildBriefStep asks
the tasks module for the task's effective grants (new op
tasks_approval_grants_effective = core grants for the task+trigger subjects
∪ the trigger's approval_grants CONFIG — a routine's definition, not an
approval artifact) instead of merging the task-row columns itself. A failed
read grants nothing: the op gates again rather than running unapproved.

Once-grant lifecycle moves with it: core once-rows deliberately outlive
dispatch so a core-side gate can spend them DURING the run (deleting them at
dispatch would have broken the connections resume this store exists for);
the write-result step now reaps whatever the run didn't spend, with the same
best-effort tolerance the old dispatch-time column clear had.

x-engenty-trigger-id joins the task lane end to end (run context → client →
PrincipalContext → gate subjects), so routine-scoped grants are spendable at
core gates too, not only in the pre-gate transport.

The legacy task-row columns are still dual-written for rollback but no
longer read anywhere; dropping them is a follow-up release.

commits.message: task approvals mint core grants the gates can spend (D2 2c)
commits.body:
A task tool approval now writes two things: the task-row string[] columns
(unchanged — the run transport the AI pre-gate reads) and a durable row in
core.approval_grants, which is what core-side gates actually consume. Until
now "approve" from the task UI only satisfied the pre-gate; any core-level
gate (the connections profile policy foremost) 202'd the retry and filed a
second request nobody connected to the first.

Two grant axes become optional, mirroring agent_goal_grants.agent_id:
- actor_id NULL: the approval names the WORK, not the worker — decided
  before the retry's principal exists.
- module_id NULL: the approval names the OPERATION; operation ids are
  globally unique, so the module adds provenance, not precision.
Either agnostic axis requires a subject (DB check + writer + reader), so a
blank check cannot be minted or honored.

Backfill migration carries pre-dual-write approvals into the core store,
guarded for installs without the tasks module. The connections resume path
deliberately does NOT dual-write — decide already minted the core grant.

commits.message: enable channels by opt-out, delete legacy channel cluster
commits.body:
Configuring a platform is now what turns the remote channel runtime on —
SLACK_BOT_TOKEN/SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET and TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN are declared by no
other feature, so their presence is an unambiguous signal of intent, and the
separate opt-in was redundant with the credential guard that already ran.
ENGENTY_REMOTE_CHANNELS_ENABLED=false remains as the kill switch, for shutting
ingress off during an incident without rotating or deleting a bot token.

Two consequences handled: the "no platform configured" branch is now the normal
state of every deployment that doesn't use remote channels, so it returns
silently instead of warning; and the outbound queue consumer keys on the runtime
having actually registered rather than on the switch, so a process with no live
Chat SDK leaves messages queued instead of failing every one.

Also deletes the legacy external-channel cluster (ai/channels.ts,
channel-interactions.ts, channel-outbound.ts, ~700 lines). Its routes were
removed in the 2026-06-20 cutover; what remained was config parsing and outbound
helpers reachable only through re-exports in ai/index.ts, with nothing calling
them. Removing it also retires a third Slack env convention (ENGENTY_AI_SLACK_*,
ENGENTY_AI_DISCORD_*, ENGENTY_AI_CHANNEL*), read nowhere else.

commits.message: authorize the destination of proactive sends
commits.body:
remote_notify took external_thread_id from its caller — for an agent that
means model output — and validated only its shape. The consumer then
parsed tenant_id and never used it, posting wherever it was told via the
platform-level bot token. module_remote.conversations(tenant_id,
external_thread_id) already records exactly which threads a tenant has
conversed in; it was simply never consulted.

Any principal with module.engenty-remote.write (including a headless
agent) could therefore post up to 4000 chars into any thread the bot can
reach — cross-tenant message injection, and an exfiltration primitive for
an agent that can read tenant data.

Gate the send on findTenantConversation() at the operation, where the auth
context lives, and carry binding_id onto the queue. The consumer now
requires binding_id, so a payload that never passed the check — a pre-fix
message still queued, or a write that bypassed the op — is refused on the
far side of the process boundary.

Also enable the remote-channel runtime by default (manifest defaultValue),
and hydrate ENGENTY_REMOTE_CHANNELS_ENABLED from platform settings: the key
is platform-configurable so the Setup UI offers it, but it was absent from
the hydration list, so toggling it there silently did nothing.

commits.message: fold connections approvals into the core store
commits.body:
The connections approval ledger (module_connections.approval_requests) was
request-only: approving a row set status='approved', emitted an event
nobody subscribed to, and unblocked nothing — the retried run filed a
fresh request and threw connection_approval_pending again. Only
grant_always changed the outcome. "Allow once" was a button that closed a
row.

Now there is one ledger and approvals actually approve:

- @engenty/approvals-sdk carries the core approval store client
  (moved from apps/core), so modules reach it without importing core.
- The connections profile policy attaches its connection context to the
  require_approval decision (new PolicyDecision.approvalContext); core's
  applyApprovalGate stores it on the ONE deduped request it files in
  core.approval_requests and emits a platform-wide `approval.requested`
  core event — replacing the module's own request write + event, which
  fired even when a grant let the call through.
- Deciding goes through the approval service: approve mints a one-shot
  core grant for the requesting principal. Both gates consume it — core's
  applyApprovalGate (already did) and now the connections-sdk executor's
  inner gate, which used to throw unconditionally.
- The owner check runs BEFORE the decide; it used to run after, so a
  non-owner's attempt burned the request and left the owner nothing to
  approve.
- The tasks module subscribes to connections.approval.decided (payload
  now carries task_id + operation_id) and resumes a task-linked blocked
  task via the existing v0.1.66 grant + re-dispatch flow.
- Migration carries still-pending rows into core; the old table stays as
  a read-only archive until a later drop.

Request TTL moves from 5 minutes to 7 days: these rows feed a durable
queue a person may open tomorrow morning, not a caller blocking on the
answer.

Smoke-verified against the dev DB end to end (request → list → decide →
grant → consume-once → race + cross-actor refusals): 11/11.

commits.message: mount channel webhooks under /ai so they ride the core gateway
commits.body:
Mastra's getWebhookRoutes() emits paths shaped for Mastra's own server
(/api/agents/…/webhook) and they were mounted verbatim on the apps/ai
Hono app. Unprefixed, the path is shadowed by core's /api/* gateway rule
— the documented gateway URL 404'd, and the webhook only worked in dev
by exposing apps/ai directly, breaking the 'apps/ai is only reachable
via the core gateway' invariant (apps/ai holds the service credential,
the Docker socket, and the sandbox mount; it must not be internet-facing).

Prefix the mount with AI_BASE_PATH so /ai/api/agents/…/webhook resolves
through the gateway's /ai proxy like every other apps/ai route; add a
regression guard that the raw Mastra path stays unmounted; point the dev
tunnel instructions at the gateway origin.

commits.message: stop in-chat secret grants from outliving their goal
commits.body:
`core.agent_goal_grants` rows were written with no expiry, and the DAL's
`revokeGoalGrants` — the reaper its own doc comment promises — has no
caller. So "yes, this agent may read that secret, for this conversation"
actually authorized every future agent on that goal, forever.

Grants now lapse after 24h. A lapsed grant re-gates the reveal and asks the
human again, which is how a secret grant should fail. The upsert no longer
ignores duplicates: with an expiry, a second approval has to renew the row
rather than skip the write and leave the human re-asked in a loop.

Reaping on goal completion is still the better fix and still owed — the
tasks module emits no event on a goal reaching a terminal status.

commits.message: one approval gate for all three transports
commits.body:
The `require_approval` branch was written out three times — invoke,
module-ops, and plugin HTTP — and the copies had drifted. The plugin-HTTP
one never recorded `policy.require_approval` and never returned
`expiresAt`, so the same blocked call produced a different audit trail and
a less useful 202 depending on which door it came through.

either "proceed" or "ask a human". Each call site keeps only its own
transport shape. Folding the remaining approval stores into this one is a
change to a single gate rather than three.

commits.message: bound and reap approval grants now that they outlive the process
commits.body:
The in-memory Map this store replaced was garbage-collected by process death,
which quietly bounded every grant it held. Durability removed that: an
"allow once" whose retry never came, or a session grant whose owner closed the
tab, would have sat in the table forever.

Grants that are not standing authorization now carry their own end (once: 1h,
session: 24h; policy keeps none, which is what standing means), and revoking a
session's token drops that session's grants immediately — logging out has to
withdraw the elevation the user consented to for that session, and a TTL is a
backstop, not the answer.

Also wires revokeApprovalGrantsForSubject, which shipped in 0d1ee9198 with no
caller.

commits.message: make approvals durable — one store for requests and grants
commits.body:
Core's approval requests and the grants they produced lived in a per-process
Map, so a restart lost every pending request and every standing "allow" a
human had already given, and a second replica never saw the first one's. This
is the D2 consolidation's first slice: core.approval_requests +
core.approval_grants, generalizing the tasks module's proven approval_grants
columns into core where evaluatePolicy can reach them.

Requests and grants are separate tables deliberately — a request is audit
history worth keeping after the fact, a grant is live authorization that gets
consumed, and collapsing them would make deleting a used grant destroy the
record. The scope enum already carries task/trigger/goal so the tasks-module
and agent_goal_grants writers can fold in later without another migration.

Two pre-existing bugs fall out on the way:
- listPending() had NO tenant filter; /api/security/approvals pulled every
  tenant's queue and narrowed it in JS afterwards. The filter is now the
  store's, and the cross-tenant superadmin queue is a separately named method
  so it cannot be reached by omitting an argument.
- decide() had no race guard, so two approvers both minted a grant. The update
  is conditioned on status = 'pending'; the loser reads back the decided row.

Tasks columns and agent_goal_grants keep their own stores this pass.

commits.message: make the turbo remote cache actually cache
commits.body:
The remote cache has been deployed and configured all along
(build-cache.engrd.xyz, TURBO_API/TURBO_TEAM/TURBO_TOKEN set), and it has been
doing almost nothing. Two independent reasons, both silent.

Uploads were timing out. turbo's default upload timeout is 60s and the largest
module artifacts — a dist/ carrying bundled .d.ts — do not finish in that. A
timed-out upload is only a WARNING:

  the cache artifact for 2a67b8ffe2730aef was too large to upload within the timeout

so the build goes green while the artifact is never written, and every later run
misses that task again, forever. Five artifacts hit this on v0.1.89 alone. Both
workflows now set TURBO_REMOTE_CACHE_UPLOAD_TIMEOUT=300.

And publish-packages.yml had no local turbo cache at all — it was the one job
without the actions/cache restore/save that ci.yml has carried since v0.1.40. On
v0.1.89 it ran 0 cache hits against 70 misses and took 26 minutes, overrunning
its 30-minute job timeout and cancelling the release's package publish. It now
restores under the same `turbo-<os>-` prefix ci.yml saves to, so it starts from
whatever main last built (a tag run may read the default branch's caches), and
saves under a `-modules` suffix so it seeds the next release without colliding
with ci.yml's immutable keys.

Worth knowing for next time: the deploy was never the missing piece. The cache
server was up, "Remote caching enabled" was printed on every run, and the thing
was still empty — because the only symptom of a failed write is a warning
nobody reads. Documented in docs/content/dev/ci-pipeline.md with the string to
grep for.

commits.message: give the supervisor app_build instead of only delegation
commits.body:
The copilot was delegation-only for app requests: build a tool, a form, a
calculator, and it was meant to hand off to engenty.app-coder. Two live runs
showed it doing something else — scaffolding files into its own workspace and
calling that an app. Nothing a user can run is ever produced there, so the
request quietly fails while looking like it succeeded.

Delegation being the only correct path made dodging it the path of least
resistance. So the correct path is now in the supervisor's own tool belt:
`app_build` is one call that creates the app, compiles it, and publishes the
live preview into the chat. Delegation remains the route for larger, iterative
builds, and AGENTS.md draws that line explicitly — along with naming the dead
ends (own-workspace files, raw catalog operations, engenty_cli, and answering
with a document that merely contains the code).

The wiring test asserts both halves: `app_build` in ENGENTY_COPILOT_TOOL_IDS
and resolvable in the builtin registry. If either drops, the dodge returns
silently.

commits.message: keep service-principal ids out of user columns
commits.body:
A headless run acts as the AI service principal, whose `principalId` is a
core.service_credential id — not a core.users row. Handlers were writing it
straight into attribution columns that carry a foreign key to core.users, so
the insert either failed the constraint or recorded a user that does not exist.

`PluginAuthContext` now carries `principalType`, plumbed from the operation
routes, and `actorUserIdFromAuth()` reads it: the principal id for a user,
null for anything else. Absent means "user" — the assumption every caller made
before service principals existed — so nothing that already worked changes.

Converted the attribution sites in tasks, triggers, offers, secrets,
knowledge-base, connections and team-hr, and the apps/ai thread/run path:
`scopeAttributionUserId` on the session scope, a nullable `createdByUserId`
through the session store and run tracker, and no `thread_participant` owner
row for a service-created thread (its principal types only cover users and
groups). The migration drops `not null` from `ai.thread.created_by_user_id`,
matching `ai.agent_run.created_by_user_id`, which has been nullable all along
— code and migration must land together or the write fails.

Triggers were the one path still writing the id raw, and the one that matters
most: `created_by_user_id` is a core.users FK on both the trigger row and every
task it materializes, and the scheduler drives exactly that path as the service
principal. Tests pin the attribution for both principal kinds there, so a
revert fails in CI rather than silently in prod.

commits.message:
fix(core): never auto-confirm supabase db reset in setup --local when non-interactive

confirmStep silently defaulted to "yes" on the DB-reset prompt whenever
isInteractiveTerminal() was false, so any non-TTY caller (Claude Code's Bash
tool, CI, etc.) ran the destructive `supabase db reset` unattended. This is
exactly how the shared engenty-local DB got wiped on 2026-08-02: a Claude
Code session ran `pnpm engenty setup --local` in a fresh worktree and it
silently reset the DB every other worktree was sharing.

Non-interactive runs now refuse and throw with clear next steps instead of
resetting, unless --yes-reset-db is passed explicitly.

commits.message:
fix(contacts): await the post-create read on the roles path

`contacts_create` returned `repo.getById(created.id) ?? created`, but
`getById` returns a Promise, so `??` tested the Promise object and the
`?? created` fallback was unreachable. When the post-create read resolves
null — scope/RLS filtering or replica lag — the handler returned null and
failed core's non-nullable `contactRecordSchema` output contract, so the
caller saw a 500 output_contract_violation even though the contact and its
roles had been written.

The happy path masked this: an async handler flattens a returned Promise,
so the existing test could not distinguish the two forms. The new test
covers the roles path with `getById` resolving null.

commits.message:
fix(apps): survive replica cold start; close app authoring to hand-driving

Two defects the live chat E2E surfaced, both of which left the user with
no App at all.

1. app-host retries a deploy once, and only on
   agentos_apps_replica_warm_timeout. agentOS hardcodes warmTimeoutMs at
   30s (no config knob); the FIRST deploy into a fresh namespace must
   cold-start an execution replica and regularly exceeds it, while the
   identical retry lands in ~1s. Every new App's first build was failing.

2. app_create / app_file_write / app_release_propose now refuse to run
   through engenty_tool_execute and name app_build instead. Building an
   App is one sequence, and only the app_build workflow publishes the
   preview artifact — an App assembled step-by-step is invisible to the
   user however well it compiles. The copilot's AGENTS.md has forbidden
   this since the workflow landed and the live run did it anyway, so it
   is enforced rather than merely stated. Reads and the human's own
   app_release_approve/_reject stay reachable.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(security): close four critical authz holes and put core back under typecheck

Acts on the four Critical findings of the 2026-08-03 agentic-infrastructure
audit, plus the quality gap that let the worst of them ship unseen.

AUTH-01 — member→admin actor tokens. `/api/auth/actor-token` checked its
capability with `caller.capabilities.some((held) => capabilityCovers(held, …))`.
`capabilityCovers` takes the granted SET and opens with `granted.includes("*")`;
handed one string that degrades into a substring test, so any held capability
merely containing an asterisk passed — and every `tenant.member` holds
`module.*`. Any member could mint an access token carrying a tenant admin's
resolved grants. The whole set now goes to the matcher once. The route is also
rate-limited (60/min per caller+IP, the ceiling `/service-token` already had)
and records a denial audit event.

AUTH-02 — durable credentials from short-lived ones. `/service-credentials`
(never expires) and `/api-tokens` (30–90 days) asked only for a valid token
plus a capability clamp — so a 900-second service token bought a permanent
credential of identical power, the exact round trip service identity exists to
prevent. Both now require the new `core.credentials.manage` (granted to
tenant.admin only), and reject any caller whose own token is derived
(service_credential / api_token): a derived credential cannot beget a
longer-lived one.

AUTH-03 — the approval gate stays. Reverted the working-tree change that
exempted agents riding the service token from the blanket escalation. Its
stated replacement, the agent escalation profile policy, was registered only
behind `ENGENTY_AGENT_ESCALATION`, which was set in no manifest and no compose
file — so the replacement gate existed nowhere and the change simply failed
open. Decision (Matthias, 2026-08-03): keep the gate AND ship the flag on, via
the env manifest and both compose files. `policy.test.ts` now records that
decision where the next person will read it.

CON-01 — App connector writes fired with nobody's approval. An engenty App
calls core with the VIEWING USER's token, so the connections gate saw a user
principal and stood aside for the AI pre-gate — which does not run outside
chat. An App declaring `gmail_send_message` just sent the mail, while the
engenty-bridge skill promised its author a `pending_approval` result. The App
proxy now marks its calls `x-engenty-call-origin: app`, core carries it as
`PrincipalContext.callOrigin`, and the connections policy treats app origin as
autonomous: durable approval request + 202, which the proxy already maps to the
promised result. Only the literal "app" is honoured, so a forged header can
never widen anything. Note the behaviour change: App writes now also obey the
connection's `autonomous_mode` clamp. Reads are untouched.

AUTH-04 — an unreadable `role` claim resolved to "service", the most capable
default; paired with `defaultCapabilities` a token naming no role at all
arrived holding module.read/write/execute. It now falls back to the
least-privileged principal.

SYS-01 — apps/core had no `typecheck` script, so `pnpm typecheck` had never
checked it, and 189 type errors accumulated behind that gap. AUTH-01 was one of
them (TS2345, on the exact line). Now at zero and wired into the existing CI
step, with no blanket suppressions: two genuine latent bugs fixed (a wrong-depth
import that silently resolved `IdentityAdminService` to nothing; a pdfjs 5
render call missing its required `canvas: null`), six dead `principal` arguments
removed from a function whose params type never had the field, and a dozen
copy-pasted registry fixtures replaced with one shared factory so the next
interface change breaks in one place instead of twelve.

Follow-up filed: CON-02, one `module.connections.write` still spans every
connector.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(connections): scope connector write authority per connector (CON-02)

Every non-read connector action mapped to the single capability
`module.connections.write`, so one grant spanned Gmail-send + Slack-post +
OneDrive-upload: a role trusted to send mail could post to your channels.
Adds `module.connections.<read|write>.<connectorId>` underneath it.

The obvious implementation would have been a bug. Making
`module.connections.write` cover `module.connections.write.gmail` reads like
natural hierarchy — "a held capability covers its sub-tree" — but
`team-chat.member` holds a bare `module.team-chat`
(modules/team-chat/src/plugin.ts), so that rule would have silently handed
every member `module.team-chat.manage`. `module.engenty-remote` is the same
shape. So the matcher learned explicit wildcards at every segment boundary
instead (`module.connections.*`, `module.connections.write.*`, where before
only the first segment wildcarded). That is purely additive — no `module.<x>.*`
grant exists today — and widening still has to be written down by a person.

The per-connector layer is therefore RESTRICTIVE rather than permissive,
following the pattern `moduleIds` and `scopes` already use in policy.ts where
empty means unrestricted: a principal naming no connector gets every connector,
so every existing grant, custom role and long-lived API token behaves exactly as
before; a principal naming one is held to it. Operation-level
`requiredCapabilities` is deliberately untouched, which is what keeps that
back-compat true — core's gate still checks the broad capability, and these say
which connectors it may be spent on.

Enforced in the connections profile policy, which is authoritative and refuses
before any connection is resolved or approval request recorded, and re-checked
in `executeConnectorAction` under the defense-in-depth doctrine already
documented there.

Made grantable, which was half the point: `registerConnectorModule` now
contributes `connections.viewer.<id>` / `connections.editor.<id>` role profiles
so an admin assigns "Connections editor — Gmail" from the roles console. The
authz capability catalog also learned to include capabilities that appear only
on role profiles — a capability that scopes rather than unlocks used to be
invisible there, and `validateCustomRole` rejected it as a typo. That fixes
`module.team-chat` too.

Verified twice: with the scope gate disabled, exactly the two "denies a write to
a connector the role does not name" tests fail while every back-compat test
still passes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message: close four critical authz holes and put core back under typecheck
commits.body:
Acts on the four Critical findings of the 2026-08-03 agentic-infrastructure
audit, plus the quality gap that let the worst of them ship unseen.

AUTH-01 — member→admin actor tokens. `/api/auth/actor-token` checked its
capability with `caller.capabilities.some((held) => capabilityCovers(held, …))`.
`capabilityCovers` takes the granted SET and opens with `granted.includes("*")`;
handed one string that degrades into a substring test, so any held capability
merely containing an asterisk passed — and every `tenant.member` holds
`module.*`. Any member could mint an access token carrying a tenant admin's
resolved grants. The whole set now goes to the matcher once. The route is also
rate-limited (60/min per caller+IP, the ceiling `/service-token` already had)
and records a denial audit event.

AUTH-02 — durable credentials from short-lived ones. `/service-credentials`
(never expires) and `/api-tokens` (30–90 days) asked only for a valid token
plus a capability clamp — so a 900-second service token bought a permanent
credential of identical power, the exact round trip service identity exists to
prevent. Both now require the new `core.credentials.manage` (granted to
tenant.admin only), and reject any caller whose own token is derived
(service_credential / api_token): a derived credential cannot beget a
longer-lived one.

AUTH-03 — the approval gate stays. Reverted the working-tree change that
exempted agents riding the service token from the blanket escalation. Its
stated replacement, the agent escalation profile policy, was registered only
behind `ENGENTY_AGENT_ESCALATION`, which was set in no manifest and no compose
file — so the replacement gate existed nowhere and the change simply failed
open. Decision (Matthias, 2026-08-03): keep the gate AND ship the flag on, via
the env manifest and both compose files. `policy.test.ts` now records that
decision where the next person will read it.

CON-01 — App connector writes fired with nobody's approval. An engenty App
calls core with the VIEWING USER's token, so the connections gate saw a user
principal and stood aside for the AI pre-gate — which does not run outside
chat. An App declaring `gmail_send_message` just sent the mail, while the
engenty-bridge skill promised its author a `pending_approval` result. The App
proxy now marks its calls `x-engenty-call-origin: app`, core carries it as
`PrincipalContext.callOrigin`, and the connections policy treats app origin as
autonomous: durable approval request + 202, which the proxy already maps to the
promised result. Only the literal "app" is honoured, so a forged header can
never widen anything. Note the behaviour change: App writes now also obey the
connection's `autonomous_mode` clamp. Reads are untouched.

AUTH-04 — an unreadable `role` claim resolved to "service", the most capable
default; paired with `defaultCapabilities` a token naming no role at all
arrived holding module.read/write/execute. It now falls back to the
least-privileged principal.

SYS-01 — apps/core had no `typecheck` script, so `pnpm typecheck` had never
checked it, and 189 type errors accumulated behind that gap. AUTH-01 was one of
them (TS2345, on the exact line). Now at zero and wired into the existing CI
step, with no blanket suppressions: two genuine latent bugs fixed (a wrong-depth
import that silently resolved `IdentityAdminService` to nothing; a pdfjs 5
render call missing its required `canvas: null`), six dead `principal` arguments
removed from a function whose params type never had the field, and a dozen
copy-pasted registry fixtures replaced with one shared factory so the next
interface change breaks in one place instead of twelve.

Follow-up filed: CON-02, one `module.connections.write` still spans every
connector.

commits.message: survive replica cold start; close app authoring to hand-driving
commits.body:
Two defects the live chat E2E surfaced, both of which left the user with
no App at all.

1. app-host retries a deploy once, and only on
   agentos_apps_replica_warm_timeout. agentOS hardcodes warmTimeoutMs at
   30s (no config knob); the FIRST deploy into a fresh namespace must
   cold-start an execution replica and regularly exceeds it, while the
   identical retry lands in ~1s. Every new App's first build was failing.

2. app_create / app_file_write / app_release_propose now refuse to run
   through engenty_tool_execute and name app_build instead. Building an
   App is one sequence, and only the app_build workflow publishes the
   preview artifact — an App assembled step-by-step is invisible to the
   user however well it compiles. The copilot's AGENTS.md has forbidden
   this since the workflow landed and the live run did it anyway, so it
   is enforced rather than merely stated. Reads and the human's own
   app_release_approve/_reject stay reachable.

commits.message: await the post-create read on the roles path
commits.body:
`contacts_create` returned `repo.getById(created.id) ?? created`, but
`getById` returns a Promise, so `??` tested the Promise object and the
`?? created` fallback was unreachable. When the post-create read resolves
null — scope/RLS filtering or replica lag — the handler returned null and
failed core's non-nullable `contactRecordSchema` output contract, so the
caller saw a 500 output_contract_violation even though the contact and its
roles had been written.

The happy path masked this: an async handler flattens a returned Promise,
so the existing test could not distinguish the two forms. The new test
covers the roles path with `getById` resolving null.

commits.message: lean projects - optional time planning, editable client
commits.body:
A project no longer has to be full-featured. `timeplan_enabled` (default true,
so every existing project keeps its Zeitplan) decides whether the project plans
time at all; with it off the project is a lean room for notes, files and tasks.

- Create dialog: wider, asks for time planning up front, with start/end date on
  one line while it is on. Dates typed and then switched off are dropped rather
  than saved invisibly.
- Project page: the Zeitplan block only renders when time planning is on, and a
  native "Time planning" tab exists only then - it renders the same shared
  section at the wide content width. It is `required` so the tabs dialog cannot
  hide it; the project setting owns it.
- Portal panel becomes the project settings panel: Client / Time planning /
  Client portal sections, each switched from its section title, body card only
  while there is something to configure.
- The client is now editable - inline on the project page and in the settings
  panel, via a shared picker. `ProjectUpdateInput` excluded `client_id`, so the
  client could only ever be set at creation; the API already accepted it.
- The team empty state always offers an add affordance: with no candidates in
  the catalog it links to the team module instead of rendering nothing.
- "Planning" tab renamed to "Overview".

commits.message: switch thumb lands flush right, long dates clip
commits.body:
The checked thumb offset was `calc(100% - 2px)` - the thumb's own width minus
2px - which only reaches the far end when 1rem is 16px. This app's root is
14px, so the thumb stopped 4px short of the right edge. Offset by the track's
content width minus the thumb instead, which is correct at any root size.

DatePicker rendered the formatted date as a bare text node in a flex button, so
it could not shrink: a long date ("August 27th, 2026") in a narrow field spilled
past the border. Wrap it in a truncating span.

commits.message: make the timeline density control a legible scale
commits.body:
The day/week/month slider read as a quantity: the filled range suggested "50%
of something" at Woche and only the current stop was labelled. Suppress the
range fill, tick every stop, and put a clickable D/W/M label on each one, all
sharing a single offset helper so ticks, labels and thumb line up (the thumb
uses `center` alignment so the outer stops sit on the track ends).

Also reset the lazily loaded range offsets when the density changes - they are
counted in the current unit, so 26 extra weeks were read as 26 extra months.
The effect meant to do this had an empty dependency array and never ran.

commits.message: keep contribution kinds the plugin pruner does not own
commits.body:
`pruneStaleUiPluginContributionsData` rebuilt `contributions` key by key and
silently dropped everything it does not prune - `liveBindings`, `brandSource`,
`copilotArticleHrefResolver`. App feeds `contributions.liveBindings` straight

the whole UI down and forced a reload.

lists. Covered by a regression test.

commits.message: never auto-confirm supabase db reset in setup --local when non-interactive
commits.body:
confirmStep silently defaulted to "yes" on the DB-reset prompt whenever
isInteractiveTerminal() was false, so any non-TTY caller (Claude Code's Bash
tool, CI, etc.) ran the destructive `supabase db reset` unattended. This is
exactly how the shared engenty-local DB got wiped on 2026-08-02: a Claude
Code session ran `pnpm engenty setup --local` in a fresh worktree and it
silently reset the DB every other worktree was sharing.

Non-interactive runs now refuse and throw with clear next steps instead of
resetting, unless --yes-reset-db is passed explicitly.

commits.message: classify output-schema mismatches as 500, not 400
commits.body:
app_call/app_call_privileged returned callApp's domain-cased {appId}
against an outputSchema requiring wire {app_id}, so every successful
app-host call failed output validation — and core's catch-all treated
that ZodError as a 400 "validation_error", making a module's own
contract breach look like broken caller input. Map the result to the
wire shape, and have executeModuleOperation/invokeOperation report
output-schema failures as 500 "output_contract_violation" instead.

commits.message: publish the app_build preview artifact to the user-facing thread
commits.body:
Inside a delegated run the ALS orchestratorThreadId is the app-coder's
CHILD thread, so publishArtifactStep scoped the app artifact where the
user never looks (the bug the first live E2E found). New ALS field
userFacingThreadId: root runs set it to their own thread, delegate-run
inherits it through the context spread, and app_build prefers it when
choosing the publish thread.

(Re-commit of 7be790c5b, which a concurrent session's reset to
origin/main undid; the AGENTS.md half of the original landed in
df3e5988a.)

commits.message:
fix(core): exempt the platform service credential from approval escalation

The generic policy gate escalated every non-user principal to
require_approval on high-risk operations. That was written for agents —
but since CP4 moved the scheduler onto the engenty service token
(principalType "service" instead of the Supabase user's "user"), the
boot reconcile's triggers_create/triggers_update and every scheduled
triggers_fire fell into the same gate. An unattended lane has no human
who could ever answer, so prod ran with zero triggers: "module trigger
create failed — routine will not run: Approval required".

Exempt exactly the platform's own lane: principalType "service" +
authMethod "service_credential" + no agent in the chain. Its authority
remains the capability clamp baked into the credential. An agent riding
the same service token (headless task runs forward x-engenty-agent-id)
keeps the escalation — the durable-approvals lane is keyed on the agent,
not the bearer — and profile policies still run first and keep the last
word.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(connections): in-chat popup connect flow for the agent connect card

The connections_request_connect chat card now drives OAuth in a popup
window instead of navigating away from the conversation: ConnectButton
gains a popup flow (window opened inside the click gesture, auth URL
assigned after fetch, redirect-fallback when blocked), the new
/connections/oauth/complete landing page reports the result to the
opener via postMessage and closes, and the card then refreshes the
connections catalog and resumes the conversation with a continuation
message. The OAuth callback carries the connector id in its redirect and
honors redirect_to on provider errors, connects emit a new
connections.connected module bus event, and connect-request tool parts
escape the collapsed tool timeline so the card always renders full-width.

commits.message:
fix(ai): thread resolveContext into the /generate assembly path

resolveAgentForSessionMemory (used by sessions.generate(), the
/threads/:id/generate route) built assembleOptions without
resolveContext, so a function agent rendered bare — no durable
agent_state store — and useThreadState setters threw
("has no durable store behind this render"). The AG-UI streaming
path (startConversationRun) already threaded this correctly since
Phase 2; this brings /generate in line.

Verified live against the engenty.issue-triage-demo phase agent: the
enter_diagnose transition tool, which failed before this fix, now
persists metadata.agent_state = {"step":"diagnose"} and the next
render picks up the diagnose phase's planning_coding model tier
(gateway/anthropic/claude-sonnet-5 vs turn 1's gpt-5-mini chat tier).

commits.message:
docs: add dev-server skill and fix the worktree first-run setup gap

New .claude/skills/dev-server/SKILL.md covers the Claude-Code-specific
mechanics of starting this repo's dev server: preview_start/launch.json
wiring (including a corepack pnpm-version PATH trap found today —
/Users/m/.nvm/.../bin/pnpm resolves the wrong pinned version outside a
login shell), the first-run pnpm engenty setup check, when not to
hand-seed a port slot, a Bash-background fallback for when preview_start
loses track of a slow multi-service startup, and the rule to always
navigate to the .localhost gateway URL rather than the raw port
preview_start auto-opens.

Also fixes a real documentation bug: both docs/dev/portless-local-urls.md
and the release skill's worktree step jumped from `pnpm install` straight
to `pnpm dev:portless --domain=x`, never mentioning `pnpm engenty setup
--local`. supabase/config.toml and the generated UI plugin catalog are
gitignored, so a fresh worktree has neither — skipping setup causes two
deferred failures (Docker port collision on :54322 from a wrong
project_id, then a later "missing generated UI plugin catalog" build
failure) that don't obviously point back to the missing step.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(ai): run the scheduler reconcile under an authenticated tools context

The boot reconcile builds its routine declarations from
moduleLoader.listModuleCapabilities(), which reads its bearer from the
Engenty-tools AsyncLocalStorage — a store only the HTTP middleware ever
entered. A reconcile has no request behind it, so step 1 threw "this run
does not include an end-user bearer token" and every later step was
skipped: no trigger and no system job got a Mastra schedule. Inbox sync,
calendar sync and interrupt cleanup were all silently unscheduled.

Enter the ALS explicitly with a freshly vended service token, per
attempt, so a retry minutes later never rides a stale one.

Pre-existing, not a CP1-CP4 regression: production had no service
credential configured until now, so the scheduler shut down at
"scheduler disabled" and never reached the reconcile.

Also stop meta from clobbering the log record in @engenty/telemetry.
`{ message: err.message }` is the convention at ~35 call sites and was
spread over the record's own message, which is why this failure printed
in production as a bare error string with no hint of what had failed.
The caller's value is kept as `detail` rather than dropped.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(db): grants coverage guard, and RLS on the last three uncovered tables

The v0.1.82 outage (four core tables unwritable by service_role) was invisible
to the test suite, because the auth stores fall back to an in-memory
implementation and no test asks Postgres whether a grant exists. This adds the
missing guard, modelled on check-rls-coverage: every table in core and module_*
must be reachable by service_role, with per-verb exceptions declared in
scripts/grants-coverage-allowlist.json.

Its first run found three more: module_kb article_versions, faq_versions and
kb_activity_log hold select+insert only — deliberate append-only tables, now
recorded as exceptions with their rationale rather than left as folklore.

Also enables RLS on core.invoices, core.satellites and
core.tenant_entitlement_overrides, the last tenant-scoped tables without it.
No behaviour change: neither anon nor authenticated holds any privilege on
them and core reaches them with the service key, so this only removes the
trapdoor where a later grant would silently expose cross-tenant rows.

Verified locally: both guards green, and a scratch table with revoked grants
is correctly reported as "missing: insert,update".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(db): grant service_role on core tables created after the baseline grant

`grant ... on all tables in schema core to service_role` in the baseline runs
~2000 lines before device_authorizations, sessions, api_tokens and
service_credential are created, and no default privileges were set — so those
four have never been writable by service_role in any environment. Device login
failed with "device_authorizations insert: permission denied", and
`engenty service-token create` failed the same way on service_credential.
module_projects.portal_rate_limits had the same gap.

Re-runs the blanket grant and adds `alter default privileges`, so tables added
from here on are covered automatically. Verified locally: the exact failing
insert now succeeds as service_role.

feat(core): durable service credentials and short-lived service tokens (CP2)

POST /api/auth/service-token exchanges a durable secret for a 15-minute
engenty access token with principalType=service. The durable half never
travels as an Authorization header, so the value that sits in an env var
is not itself a session — which is the whole point of the change.

Adds core.service_credential, the auth-store pair (memory + supabase),
CRUD routes clamped to the creator's capabilities and tenant, and
`engenty service-token create|list|revoke`.

feat(setup): show the OAuth redirect URI and deploy-env status on /setup/platform

Operators had to derive the connector callback URL from the manifest's
`<ENGENTY_API_BASE_URL>` placeholder, and env-only deploy keys were invisible
until a flow failed in the container logs.

- resolve the placeholder server-side and render each provider's steps
- show the exact redirect URI per OAuth group, with copy-to-clipboard
- honour CONNECTIONS_REDIRECT_URI (not DB-configurable, so read from env)
- warn on *.localhost redirect hosts, which providers reject, and offer the
  loopback URL derived from ENGENTY_CORE_BASE_URL
- report deploy-scope, non-configurable keys as read-only Set/Not-set rows
  (values never leave the server) so a missing one surfaces before it breaks

commits.message:
ci: reach Coolify over HTTPS when SSH is firewalled

The deploy job was SSH-only on the premise that port 22 was not
IP-allowlisted while the HTTP API was. That premise is false: since
v0.1.79 the runners time out connecting to 22, while the same host
answers on 22 and 443 instantly from the operator's address.

Try the Coolify API first when COOLIFY_API_TOKEN is set, and fall back
to the existing forced-command SSH key otherwise. 443 is the one port
that cannot be closed to the runners without also locking the operator
out of the panel, so it is the more durable route. The response body is
printed on failure because the status code is what distinguishes a bad
token from an allowlist from a wrong uuid.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(deploy): give edge the app-host URL and token

The modules/engenty-apps plugin loads in core, not only in apps/ai, and
it is the half that builds and calls deployed apps. Both compose files
passed ENGENTY_APP_HOST_URL/TOKEN to engenty-ai and engenty-app-host but
not to engenty-edge, so production booted with

  "ENGENTY_APP_HOST_URL unset - app builds and app calls are unavailable"

and every app build failed while app-host itself looked fine. Pass both
to edge as well.

commits.message:
feat(ai): self-renewing service credential for headless runs

The scheduler, task dispatcher and remote channels all rode a Supabase
access token frozen into ENGENTY_AI_SERVICE_JWT at deploy time. Access
tokens expire by design — an hour on hosted Supabase — so scheduled
triggers silently died when the token did, and production has never had
a working way to set one.

Hold the durable credential instead: ENGENTY_AI_SERVICE_EMAIL/PASSWORD
(the service@engenty.local identity pnpm service:jwt already
provisions). A small vendor (apps/ai/src/ai/service-credential.ts)
signs in via password grant, caches the session, re-mints inside a
120s expiry margin, and shares one in-flight sign-in across concurrent
callers. Tokens are fetched per fire/dispatch, never captured at boot,
so a fire days after boot cannot ride a dead token. Revocation is the
identity itself: disable the service user and the next mint fails.

ENGENTY_AI_SERVICE_JWT still wins when set (local dev, escape hatch).
A configured-but-failing credential lands in the scheduler's retry
path, not its disabled path — a transient Supabase hiccup at boot must
not permanently disable triggers.

Both compose files now actually pass the credential vars to engenty-ai
(the JWT var was never plumbed through, which is why production could
only warn). mint-service-jwt.mjs persists the email/password pair to
.env.local — it resets the password on every run, so an operator who
copied it into production must know a re-run invalidated it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(deploy): verify the agentos-apps patch without require.resolve

Second reason app-host has never built. @rivet-dev/agentos-apps declares no
`main`, and its `exports["."]` map defines only an `import` condition, so a CJS
`require.resolve` throws ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED before it ever reads the
file. The guard could not pass whether or not the patch applied — it simply

commits.message:
feat(ai): govern model selection through one shared allow-list

Four places decided whether a model was legal, each with its own untrimmed
`Array.includes`, and they disagreed. The picker filtered, the resolver
demoted, the preflight rejected, and agent assembly checked nothing at all.

- `isModelAllowed` in ai-core is now the single definition, shared by the
  picker, the purpose resolver, the usage preflight and agent assembly.
  Comparison is canonical (trimmed, lowercased) but never strips path
  segments: a routing-prefixed id bills differently from the bare one.
- Resolution can no longer return a model the preflight will reject. The
  env and package-default layers were previously exempt from the allow-list,
  so a tenant whose list omitted the platform default got `model_not_allowed`
  on every turn — and the picker only offers granted models, leaving no way
  out from inside the product. Resolution now falls back to a granted model.
- Per-agent pins go through the same check. `resolveAgentModelId` returned
  `modelOverride` verbatim, and sub-agents never reach the preflight, so a
  pinned sub-agent ran whatever it named. Grants ride on RuntimeModelConfig
  so this costs no extra policy read per assembled agent.
- New `allowed_providers` grants a whole vendor. Model-id lists go stale on
  every vendor release; a provider grant does not. The two lists are additive.
- Entitlement propagation no longer swallows its errors, and a new re-apply
  route rolls a package's policy out to tenants already assigned to it —
  previously nothing re-ran, so package edits never reached them.
- Authored packages now seed `core.packages` only when a row is absent. A
  version bump used to overwrite operator edits on the next boot, silently.

Two tests changed meaning rather than being patched: one was named "does not
filter platform/default values against the allow-list" and encoded the bug;
the other expected a 429 where the tenant had granted the model being asked
for, which was the lockout itself.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(manage): add AI model console and allow-list editors

The superadmin routes for the gateway model catalog, sync and availability
have existed since the manage-app rewrite, but nothing called them: the page
was dropped in the port and never rebuilt. Same for the tenant usage-policy
admin route, whose own comment calls manage "the canonical central-write
path". A tenant whose policy is `managed_by='entitlement'` therefore had an
allow-list that no interface could edit — the tenant UI answers 409 and manage
had no UI at all.

- New /ai-models console: sync now, sync-run history (the legacy page fetched
  runs but only ever showed the latest), catalog with server-side filters and
  search, per-row and bulk activation deriving all six purposes from
  `use_cases`, pricing history, restore-defaults.
- Transport: manage had no way to reach the AI service. `requestAi` skips
  core's `{ data }` envelope, and a `/ai` dev proxy entry was missing entirely,
  so any such call 404'd outside production.
- Allow-list entry is canonicalised on save to match backend comparison. Free
  text is how `openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-safeguard-20b` — an id the catalog has
  never contained — ended up in a live policy where it can never match.
- Provider grants surfaced on the tenant and package views, and entitlement
  writes now report `policySynced: false` instead of implying success.

`packages.detail.authoredHint` is rewritten: packages are no longer overwritten
from code on every boot, so "defined in code and synced" was no longer true.

The one-line `$200` -> `$200.00` fix in TenantsListPage.test.tsx duplicates an
uncommitted fix in the primary checkout; identical content, so it merges clean.

commits.message:
feat(ai): resolve models from role bindings instead of env and constants

Phase 1 of the settings redesign. A role is a job a model does; a binding says
which model currently does it. The point is to stop model ids travelling: they
belong in the catalog and the binding table, and nowhere else.

- `ai.model_binding` (scope, role) -> model_id + gateway. Seeded on every boot
  with roles that have never been bound, so a role added in a later release
  needs no migration and an operator's binding is never reasserted over.
- The graded general-purpose role is `model.low` / `model.medium` /
  `model.high`, deliberately not `chat`: the same role serves tasks and agents.
  Fixed roles (router, safeguard, research, planning_coding) keep their names.
- `resolvePurposeModel` takes the bound model as its platform layer and stops
  reading env once a role is bound. The legacy `AI_*_MODEL` vars are read
  exactly once, by the seed, so an existing deployment keeps its models across
  the upgrade and there is one place to look afterwards.
- `ENGENTY_AI_DEV_MODELS=true` bypasses the allow-list at resolution so the
  whole catalog is testable. The usage preflight still enforces, so dev mode
  cannot bill an unlicensed model in production.
- Role ids are plain strings, not a closed union, because modules will declare
  their own (`coder.plan`) and the platform must not need to know what jobs a
  module invents.

Also corrects `DEFAULT_AI_SAFEGUARD_MODEL_ID`, which was
`openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-safeguard-20b` — a two-slash id that is not a valid
gateway model id and that the catalog has never contained. We do not use
OpenRouter; the model is served as `openai/gpt-oss-safeguard-20b`. Dormant
rather than live, since no agent currently enables guardrails.

The seed constants move to `model-defaults.ts` so the role catalogue and the
purpose resolver can both import them without a cycle.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(ai): plans grant effort tiers instead of enumerating model ids

Phase 3. A model-id allow-list goes stale the moment a vendor ships anything:
every release means re-listing every tenant, and one that gets missed silently
loses access to the current generation. An effort grant does not — a model bound
to `model.high` tomorrow is covered by today's grant, because the grant talks
about the job rather than the instrument.

- `allowed_efforts` on the package policy and on `ai.tenant_usage_policy`.
  NULL/empty = every tier, matching how the two model lists already read.
- Requests above the ceiling degrade downward rather than failing: a tenant on
  a low-only plan who asks for high gets low and an answer. A plan boundary
  should be a product tier, not an error — and the request is already paid for
  by the time we know the tier is too high.
- `ceilingEffort` gives the router something to size against once `auto` lands.
- Seeded plans: free = low, team = low+medium, business and enterprise
  unrestricted.

`allowed_models` and `allowed_providers` survive as the self-hosted and
expert-mode escape hatch. They are no longer the path a commercial tenant walks.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(ai): let modules declare the model roles they need

Phase 5. A module that wants its own model — a coder planning with one model and
editing with another, an OCR pass needing vision — previously had to hard-code
an id or push a new platform-wide purpose. Both make the platform responsible
for knowing what jobs a module invents.

`AiRegistration.model_roles` lets a module declare the role and a seed model;
the boot seed merges them into the platform set, so a module installed later
gets its roles bound on the next start without a migration of its own. The
binding console shows `declaredBy`, so a role's origin is visible.

A module cannot redefine a platform role: shipping a `router` role would
silently retarget every routing call in the product. Module-vs-module
collisions resolve first-declaration-wins — arbitrary, but deterministic and
visible rather than order-dependent.

commits.message:
feat(ai): make the gateway a column behind an adapter interface

Phase 2. `ai.gateway_model` becomes `ai.model` with a `gateway` column and a
`(gateway, model_id)` key, and the Vercel-specific fetch/normalize moves behind
a `ModelGateway` adapter with a registry.

Encoding the route inside the identifier is what produced ids like
`openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-safeguard-20b` — three segments, where every real
catalog row has exactly two, so nothing could ever match it. Making the gateway
a column removes that class of bug rather than papering over an instance of it,
and is what lets a second gateway exist at all: adding OpenRouter is one adapter
file and one line in the registry, with no change to resolution.

The sync stamps the gateway itself rather than trusting the adapter, so no
adapter can write into another's rows, and it keeps deriving price tiers
locally since that classification is ours and not the gateway's. Pricing
inserts still dedupe by model id because `ai.model_pricing` has no gateway
column — worth revisiting when a model is served by two gateways at different
prices.

No compatibility view: the only reader was the AI store, which moves with the
migration, and a view cannot take the `ON CONFLICT` the upsert needs. The
migration ends with a PostgREST schema reload because a rename changes what is
exposed. Rollback is symmetric and lossless.

Verified on the live local database: 323 rows survived with gateway='vercel'
and activation flags intact.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
feat(ai): effort selector replaces the model picker

Phase 4, and the wiring that finally makes phase 3's grants do something.

End users now choose how much thinking a task deserves — low, medium, high or
auto — instead of picking from three hundred model ids. The choice travels as
`forwardedProps.engenty.effort` alongside `model_id`, never replacing it, and
the backend turns it into a model through the graded role binding, clamped to
what the plan grants. A tenant on a low-only plan who asks for high gets low and
an answer; a plan boundary should be a product tier, not an error, and the
request is already paid for by the time we know the tier is too high.

An explicit `model_id` still wins, because expert and self-hosted installs pin
models deliberately. The model chooser is not deleted — it moved behind an
expert toggle in the composer, and the per-purpose matrix behind one on
/settings/ai. Leaving expert mode clears the pin so a stale one cannot outlive
the switch.

`auto` is accepted on the wire but not yet acted on: router-sized effort still
needs the router to run, and treating it as "no pick" degrades to the tenant
default rather than guessing.

Three gaps left deliberately, each needing a decision rather than more code:
- `GET /ai/v1/usage/policy` is tenant-admin only, so a non-admin composer sees
  all four tiers offered. The service clamps regardless, so this is cosmetic —
  but it needs a member-scoped read of `allowed_efforts` to look right.
- Per-agent effort does not persist yet; the agents tab round-trips to
  "inherit" until `PATCH /ai/registry/agents/:id` accepts an `effort` column.
- Tasks expose no model choice today, so none was added.

commits.message:
fix(core): make the model-gateway migration re-runnable

Postgres has no `ADD CONSTRAINT IF NOT EXISTS` and no
`RENAME CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS`, so three statements in this migration could only
ever run once. A failure in any later statement left the file permanently
unrunnable: the retry died on the primary key the first attempt had already
created, with the table half-renamed. Every other statement here was already
guarded, which made the gap easy to miss.

Found the hard way — the migration had been applied out-of-band, so the real
run replayed it and wedged on exactly that statement.

Verified by replaying the whole file against a database already in the target
state: no error, 323 rows and the (gateway, model_id) key intact.

commits.message:
feat(manage): add the role binding console

The missing half of the roles work. Phase 1 shipped the binding table, the boot
seed and the resolver, so the platform knew which model does which job — but
nothing in the product could show or change it. "Where is it defined which model
is used?" was answerable only by opening psql. That is not a design, it is an
omission, and it made the tenant-facing effort screen look like it had lost the
setting rather than moved it.

- `GET /ai/v1/models/bindings` joins the role catalogue with what is actually
  bound, so a role that has never been bound still appears with its seed shown.
  Listing only bound rows would hide precisely the roles someone needs to fix.
- `PATCH /ai/v1/models/bindings/:role` refuses unknown roles rather than storing
  them: a typo would otherwise sit in the table looking authoritative while
  nothing ever read it.
- Superadmin-only, under Settings -> AI models -> Role bindings, split into the
  graded roles users choose between and the specialist roles they never see.
  Module-declared roles show which module declared them.

commits.message:
fix(ai): isolate the placeholder session workspace per user

Runs whose agent has no workspace of its own were handed a single memoised
`Workspace` rooted at one `tmpdir()` path — every tenant in the process on the
same directory. Nothing mounts that workspace today, so nothing leaked, but it
was a cross-tenant file surface waiting for the first tool that did.

Now rooted per user. The id is sanitised before it reaches a path, since it
composes into one.

Worth recording: a workspace with no filesystem at all would be better, and
`WorkspaceConfig` makes every field optional — but the constructor rejects it at
runtime ("requires at least a filesystem, sandbox, or skills"), and an empty
skills array does not satisfy it either. A single inert skill does, but its
visibility to the model is a behaviour change rather than a fix. The test
asserts the rejection, so if that constraint ever lifts the placeholder can go.

This path had no test coverage at all, which is how the shared instance went
unnoticed.

commits.message:
test(ai): give the two heavyweight smoke tests a real budget

Both stand up genuine machinery — a Mastra instance with mounted channel routes,
and the scheduler heartbeat wiring. Together they run in ~5s alone, but a single
one of these files takes 10-13s when the parallel forks are competing for CPU,
which pushed them past the 10s global budget. The result looked exactly like a
race: a different test failing each run, each passing in isolation.

Widened only on the two tests whose cost is real and understood, so a genuine
hang anywhere else still trips the default.

Verified by three consecutive runs of the combination that reproduced it.

commits.message:
feat(apps): app-build workflow — the durable sequence behind app_build

The chat E2E proved the build sequence cannot live in the model: across
approval interruptions it lost its own app_id and created three duplicate
apps, and its "show me" step pasted the source into an html artifact
instead of publishing the app handle. The same division of labour agentOS
draws with workflow()/ctx.step() now applies here: the pipeline is code,
the agent authors files and reads build logs.

New Mastra workflow `app-build` (ensure-app → write-files → propose →
publish-artifact), registered beside task-job. ensure-app finds by slug
before creating, so a fix-loop retry lands on the same app. A failed
build is a normal outcome carrying the verbatim build_log, not an error.
The publish step pins the `app` artifact to the version just built — the
user previews exactly what they then approve. Activation stays a
human-governed operation; the workflow never calls app_release_approve.

Steps ride the caller's own bearer via the tools ALS when run from chat
(never persisted into the snapshot) and fall back to the tenant-checked
service principal headlessly — the task-job seam, reused.

The agent surface narrows accordingly: app-coder declares the new
`app_build` tool and its instructions forbid driving the raw operations
by hand; the copilot's supervisor rules route app requests to
engenty.app-coder. A wiring test asserts every tool id in the app-coder
manifest resolves in the builtin registry.

commits.message:
fix(copilot): give the supervisor an agent-app_coder delegation tool

AGENTS.md has told the copilot to delegate app-build requests to
engenty.app-coder since the app_build workflow landed, but the delegate
tools are built one-per-entry from the static subAgents array, which only
listed engenty.cli and file_analyst. So agent-app_coder never existed and
the model reached for the closest thing it had: the sandboxed CLI agent,
which has no App tooling. A live "build me a shopping-list app" chat came
back with a hand-written localStorage preview.html and zero rows in
module_apps.apps.

engenty.app-coder is module-provided rather than builtin, but production
assembles the copilot with skipSubAgents and resolves each delegate lazily
inside its tool call, so a tenant without engenty-apps active degrades to
a failed tool call rather than a broken chat. The two unit tests that do
resolve the tree eagerly stub the config to match an active tenant.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message:
fix(deploy): copy patches before pnpm fetch so images build again

Every deploy image build has failed since v0.1.75 — v0.1.74 was the last one to
produce images. Three releases went out with nothing deployed behind them.

`pnpm fetch` resolves from pnpm-lock.yaml, which records the patched
@rivet-dev/agentos-apps dependency, so it needs patches/ on disk. All three
fetch-based images copied it afterwards (app-host) or never (ai, edge), and died
with ERR_PNPM_PATCH_NOT_FOUND. sandbox and migrate were unaffected, which is why
the run looked partially healthy.

Verified by building the ai image's deps stage locally, which previously failed
at exactly this step.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.message: make the model-gateway migration re-runnable
commits.body:
Postgres has no `ADD CONSTRAINT IF NOT EXISTS` and no
`RENAME CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS`, so three statements in this migration could only
ever run once. A failure in any later statement left the file permanently
unrunnable: the retry died on the primary key the first attempt had already
created, with the table half-renamed. Every other statement here was already
guarded, which made the gap easy to miss.

Found the hard way — the migration had been applied out-of-band, so the real
run replayed it and wedged on exactly that statement.

Verified by replaying the whole file against a database already in the target
state: no error, 323 rows and the (gateway, model_id) key intact.

commits.message: effort selector replaces the model picker
commits.body:
Phase 4, and the wiring that finally makes phase 3's grants do something.

End users now choose how much thinking a task deserves — low, medium, high or
auto — instead of picking from three hundred model ids. The choice travels as
`forwardedProps.engenty.effort` alongside `model_id`, never replacing it, and
the backend turns it into a model through the graded role binding, clamped to
what the plan grants. A tenant on a low-only plan who asks for high gets low and
an answer; a plan boundary should be a product tier, not an error, and the
request is already paid for by the time we know the tier is too high.

An explicit `model_id` still wins, because expert and self-hosted installs pin
models deliberately. The model chooser is not deleted — it moved behind an
expert toggle in the composer, and the per-purpose matrix behind one on
/settings/ai. Leaving expert mode clears the pin so a stale one cannot outlive
the switch.

`auto` is accepted on the wire but not yet acted on: router-sized effort still
needs the router to run, and treating it as "no pick" degrades to the tenant
default rather than guessing.

Three gaps left deliberately, each needing a decision rather than more code:
- `GET /ai/v1/usage/policy` is tenant-admin only, so a non-admin composer sees
  all four tiers offered. The service clamps regardless, so this is cosmetic —
  but it needs a member-scoped read of `allowed_efforts` to look right.
- Per-agent effort does not persist yet; the agents tab round-trips to
  "inherit" until `PATCH /ai/registry/agents/:id` accepts an `effort` column.
- Tasks expose no model choice today, so none was added.

commits.message: make the gateway a column behind an adapter interface
commits.body:
Phase 2. `ai.gateway_model` becomes `ai.model` with a `gateway` column and a
`(gateway, model_id)` key, and the Vercel-specific fetch/normalize moves behind
a `ModelGateway` adapter with a registry.

Encoding the route inside the identifier is what produced ids like
`openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-safeguard-20b` — three segments, where every real
catalog row has exactly two, so nothing could ever match it. Making the gateway
a column removes that class of bug rather than papering over an instance of it,
and is what lets a second gateway exist at all: adding OpenRouter is one adapter
file and one line in the registry, with no change to resolution.

The sync stamps the gateway itself rather than trusting the adapter, so no
adapter can write into another's rows, and it keeps deriving price tiers
locally since that classification is ours and not the gateway's. Pricing
inserts still dedupe by model id because `ai.model_pricing` has no gateway
column — worth revisiting when a model is served by two gateways at different
prices.

No compatibility view: the only reader was the AI store, which moves with the
migration, and a view cannot take the `ON CONFLICT` the upsert needs. The
migration ends with a PostgREST schema reload because a rename changes what is
exposed. Rollback is symmetric and lossless.

Verified on the live local database: 323 rows survived with gateway='vercel'
and activation flags intact.

commits.message: let modules declare the model roles they need
commits.body:
Phase 5. A module that wants its own model — a coder planning with one model and
editing with another, an OCR pass needing vision — previously had to hard-code
an id or push a new platform-wide purpose. Both make the platform responsible
for knowing what jobs a module invents.

`AiRegistration.model_roles` lets a module declare the role and a seed model;
the boot seed merges them into the platform set, so a module installed later
gets its roles bound on the next start without a migration of its own. The
binding console shows `declaredBy`, so a role's origin is visible.

A module cannot redefine a platform role: shipping a `router` role would
silently retarget every routing call in the product. Module-vs-module
collisions resolve first-declaration-wins — arbitrary, but deterministic and
visible rather than order-dependent.

commits.message: plans grant effort tiers instead of enumerating model ids
commits.body:
Phase 3. A model-id allow-list goes stale the moment a vendor ships anything:
every release means re-listing every tenant, and one that gets missed silently
loses access to the current generation. An effort grant does not — a model bound
to `model.high` tomorrow is covered by today's grant, because the grant talks
about the job rather than the instrument.

- `allowed_efforts` on the package policy and on `ai.tenant_usage_policy`.
  NULL/empty = every tier, matching how the two model lists already read.
- Requests above the ceiling degrade downward rather than failing: a tenant on
  a low-only plan who asks for high gets low and an answer. A plan boundary
  should be a product tier, not an error — and the request is already paid for
  by the time we know the tier is too high.
- `ceilingEffort` gives the router something to size against once `auto` lands.
- Seeded plans: free = low, team = low+medium, business and enterprise
  unrestricted.

`allowed_models` and `allowed_providers` survive as the self-hosted and
expert-mode escape hatch. They are no longer the path a commercial tenant walks.

commits.message: resolve models from role bindings instead of env and constants
commits.body:
Phase 1 of the settings redesign. A role is a job a model does; a binding says
which model currently does it. The point is to stop model ids travelling: they
belong in the catalog and the binding table, and nowhere else.

- `ai.model_binding` (scope, role) -> model_id + gateway. Seeded on every boot
  with roles that have never been bound, so a role added in a later release
  needs no migration and an operator's binding is never reasserted over.
- The graded general-purpose role is `model.low` / `model.medium` /
  `model.high`, deliberately not `chat`: the same role serves tasks and agents.
  Fixed roles (router, safeguard, research, planning_coding) keep their names.
- `resolvePurposeModel` takes the bound model as its platform layer and stops
  reading env once a role is bound. The legacy `AI_*_MODEL` vars are read
  exactly once, by the seed, so an existing deployment keeps its models across
  the upgrade and there is one place to look afterwards.
- `ENGENTY_AI_DEV_MODELS=true` bypasses the allow-list at resolution so the
  whole catalog is testable. The usage preflight still enforces, so dev mode
  cannot bill an unlicensed model in production.
- Role ids are plain strings, not a closed union, because modules will declare
  their own (`coder.plan`) and the platform must not need to know what jobs a
  module invents.

Also corrects `DEFAULT_AI_SAFEGUARD_MODEL_ID`, which was
`openrouter/openai/gpt-oss-safeguard-20b` — a two-slash id that is not a valid
gateway model id and that the catalog has never contained. We do not use
OpenRouter; the model is served as `openai/gpt-oss-safeguard-20b`. Dormant
rather than live, since no agent currently enables guardrails.

The seed constants move to `model-defaults.ts` so the role catalogue and the
purpose resolver can both import them without a cycle.
